body.text: Thursday’s seminar will not meet. I shall be in Berkeley, the city, giving a lecture to people who have paid to disagree with me. The dog remains in Marisol with Mr. Marsh. For Monday, everyone: Percy, *The Moviegoer*. Those of you who will be in Louisiana may read it there and write to me about its accuracy. —A.H.

body: *Berkeley, the city*, to tell it apart from Berkeley, the dog, who stays; Jack can hear the clause in Hale’s vowels, tucked in at the corners like a hospital bed. And then *those of you.* As far as Jack knows, Hale has twelve students and no information, and that has never slowed him down. Jack hasn’t asked him for the week yet. Office hours are nine to ten and the man flies at eleven, so the asking will have to be done at a trot.

Across the room the RAZR begins to buzz its way sideways along Jack’s desk toward the mug, and the outside screen lights with a 504 number he doesn’t know. Behind him Theo’s breathing, for hours the breathing of a sleeping man, becomes the breathing of a man imitating one. The blanket climbs to cover the other ear.
Jack gets there before the mug does and flips it open. “Hello?”
“*Bonjour, le garçon de l’Ohio.* You know who this is.”

body.text: He is standing in his socks on the cold floor, at very nearly attention, in the posture of a fourth-grader at St. Brigid’s being asked the Commandments in order. He knows the voice. He has heard it twice, both times through Lena’s phone: on the speaker in the Fishbowl kitchen in November, informing him he was skinny, and for ten seconds over break, asking was he eating.

body: “Yes, ma’am.”
“Nine o’clock here, and you sound like you’re still in the bed.”
“It’s seven here, ma’am.”
“Seven.” A lid goes down onto a pot, thoughtfully, in Louisiana. “*Bon.* Seven’s not early. By seven I’ve won my first argument.” Then: “You remember what I told you.”
“Come to this house first.”

“*Bon.*” Behind her something is being chopped on a board, steadily, by a person with a grievance, and an AM radio is discussing the Saints at length and in several accents. “*La rousse* gave me this number. The redhead. She calls Celeste every night now. I don’t know what for. Celeste says she’s *organized*.”

Jack holds the RAZR out and looks at it. Laney Price has been saying *Jack* to him with nothing on it, at civil intervals, for a month. It appears she has also been working the long-distance lines to Dupre Street. “Yes, ma’am,” he says.

“Wednesday you said no. I do not ask why; a person’s why is his own. Wednesday night you said yes. I do not ask that either. The redhead told Celeste, and Celeste told me before her coffee.” It is accurate to the hour. Apparently he is news in Louisiana. The chopping stops. “So you have said yes to the rich boy, and I am calling anyway. You don’t come because the rich boy asked you. You come because I asked you.”
“Yes, ma’am. I’ll —”
“Don’t bring nothing.”
“Ma’am, I can’t show up at somebody’s house with —”
“You bring something, Celeste has to find a place to put it. You bring yourself. You eat. You go to Mass with us Sunday. You eat shrimp?”
“I eat what’s on the table, ma’am.”
“That is the right answer.” A spoon rings off a rim. “We will see if it is the true one. Thirty hours, Celeste says. In a Honda.”
“It’s a minivan, ma’am. It’s a very good one.”

“In my day we drove to Lafayette and it was a vacation.” Jack has never seen that kitchen and could draw it: the onions going clear in the iron pot, the cayenne tin, a stove that was old when Tony was a boy. The chopping starts again, harder. “Tony has been sick to his stomach since the Vikings. Since *January.* I told him, Tony, it is a game, and he looked at me like I said something about his mother. Sunday I do not care who wins. I care who is at my table.” The board goes quiet. “I told Magdalena I was calling you. She said, *Mémère, don’t.*” The spoon taps the rim twice. “So.”
Which settles whose invitation it is, and he has had worse news from better sources. On Dupre Street a pot is waiting, and he has about a second and a half.

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first. Thursday at seven in the morning she called me herself, from Dupre Street, on a number the redhead gave her. She knew I’d said yes. She called anyway: I don’t come because the rich boy asked me, I come because she asked me. Don’t bring nothing. Come to this house first — I said it back to her. Lena told her not to call.

response: “I know you will. I’m the one who said it.” Then, away from the phone and at three times the volume, in French: not the big pot, the other one, and who has touched her roux. A lid rings down. The line is a kitchen for a moment, and then it is nothing at all, and Jack is left with “Thank you, ma’am, I’ll —” in his mouth and no one to put it to.
“Who was that?” Theo asks, from under the blanket.
“Lena’s grandmother.”
“Oh, *really*,” says the blanket, and goes to sleep at once, unconvincingly: it begins to snore, in the wrong key. On the nightstand Hollis, in his teacup, keeps his own counsel.

Then she is shouting at someone in the yard, in French, about a chicken, and the screen door slaps for real, and the call is the sound of Dupre Street in the morning, and then not even that.
Theo is up on one elbow, hair in every direction. “Who was that?”
“Lena’s grandmother.”
Theo laughs once, into the pillow, and lies back down, and is asleep at once, with one eye not entirely shut.

response: “I know. Now you said it to me.” Far back in the house, a voice that must be Celeste’s asks who is on the phone, and Mémère, without covering anything, says, “*Le garçon,*” like a delivery. “Thank you, ma’am, I’ll see —” Jack says, and Celeste says something else, and the line goes to the kitchen and then to nothing.
“Who was that?” Theo asks. He has not moved.
“Lena’s grandmother.”
Theo says nothing at all. After a moment his breath evens out into sleep so promptly that a stranger could have heard it was fake from the hall.

s02.slug: THURSDAY · 9:20 AM · HOLLIS HALL, 314 — HALE’S OFFICE
body: The leaf blower on the quad has been at it since eight, one man shoving the same drift of eucalyptus bark from one side of the walk to the other, and through the window of Hollis 314 the Pacific is doing its morning silver as though nothing had happened to anybody. Jack has read the card on the glass twice on his way in and is still not sure it’s a joke.

body: The wine stain is still shaped like Italy. The leash hangs on its hook. Under the desk Berkeley’s blanket is empty and the long dent in it has gone shallow, and Hale, in the green tie, soup and all, is packing a satchel with the speed of a man who has left better cities than this one: a blue folder, a toothbrush in its own leather sleeve, a shirt he smooths once with the flat of his hand.
“Mr. Costigan.” He doesn’t look up. “You’ve come about the plural.”
“You wrote ‘those of you who will be in Louisiana.’” Jack stops just inside the door. “I hadn’t asked yet.”
“You’ve been asking since you read it. Ask, then, and briefly. I have a taxi at ten past and a lecture to finish in the back of it.”
“How’s Berkeley?” Jack says first, because the blanket is empty and somebody ought to.

“The city is flourishing and insufferable, and I am flying to it at eleven. You mean the dog.” Hale rolls a pair of socks. “With Mr. Marsh. Mr. Marsh reads to him. Kierkegaard, aloud. The dog has never been happier and can’t hear a word.” He rolls another pair. “He has put it behind him, which is a method I commend to the rest of us.”

Jack gets the picture at once: Evan Marsh at the kitchen table with his glasses on, doing *Fear and Trembling* in his seminar voice to a deaf greyhound under the same kitchen table. That is as near to Wednesday as Hale means to come, and Jack, who is done with Wednesday, leaves it where Hale put it.
Hale points the toothbrush at the other chair. Jack takes the edge of it, bag on his knees, hands out of his pockets, the nuns’ habit.

“I need the week.” He worked it out on the walk over and gives it in order. “Monday the eighth. Thursday the eleventh. Monday the fifteenth is Presidents’ Day, so that one’s a gift. Thursday the eighteenth. Three seminars. It’s the Super Bowl, or the city for it. A van, thirty hours, six people, a seating chart with a legend.”
Hale hears out the arithmetic to the eighteenth. Then, as if it were a footnote he was checking: “And who invited you? Or did you invite yourself?”
“A grandmother. She called at seven this morning.”
“Then it’s closed.” He wedges the shirt down the side of the satchel. “A grandmother is the one invitation that is also a summons.”
Against Jack’s hip the RAZR goes off, and he has it half out of the pocket before he remembers the room.
“Answer it,” Hale says, “or I shall have to listen to it die.”

body: “Did he.” Hale puts down the toothbrush. He pushes his glasses up into his hair and studies the ceiling, and almost smiles. Jack has seen him do that perhaps twice. “That’s very good. I’ll take it. Four thousand, and not one of them liminal. For years I have waited for someone to forbid it in writing. It is the most overworked bollocks in the humanities, Mr. Costigan, and half this campus has liminal’d itself into an early grave. Tell Mr. Vance that in my experience the difference between a lie and a prophecy is one of timing.”
“Is it a grade?”
“It is an essay. I find the distinction restful.”
“I’ve already got the first sentence,” Jack says. “The band goes out slow and comes back loose.”

“That is the whole thing, and you have spent it on the first line.” Hale lifts the flap again. “Mine is longer. They take their dead to the cemetery behind a brass band playing a dirge, and on the way home the band plays something else and the whole street dances.” The Housman goes in on top of the folder. “It is the only Christian thing I have ever envied.”
He turns to the shelf.
What comes down is an old paperback, the spine gone white in creases, the pages swollen from being read in a bath, *The Moviegoer*, with pencil down every margin in a small upright hand.

“Percy was a physician. He caught consumption, lay in a sanatorium reading Kierkegaard, and was received into the Church, which I hold against him. The book I forgive.” He holds it out. “It’s set there. It ends on Ash Wednesday. Mind the margins. They’re mine and they’re younger than I am. It’s Monday’s reading anyway, so you’ll have a head start. Read it in the passenger seat, Mr. Costigan. Never in the one with the wheel.”

Jack has read it. A copy came in the mail before Christmas and is on the shelf over his desk in 412, somebody else’s pencil down the middle of it to the last page. He doesn’t mention it. Hale can keep his head start.

Jack opens it at random. Beside a paragraph about a sunset Hale has written *Quite*, and three pages on, *Quite not*. It goes into his back pocket, and the Chesterton comes out of the pocket and into his bag to make room.
“Thirty hours in a motorcar with your contemporaries,” Hale says, doing up the buckles at last. “I should like to be the luggage.”
Down on the drive a taxi gives one apologetic honk.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. When Lena and I went at each other across his table he stood up and stopped it, in a voice I’ve never heard out of him, and he wasn’t amused. Berkeley felt it through the floor. On the deck he said the table was his. He asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog. He may like to do it again. Monday he gave us Joyce, “The Dead,” and taught it as if Wednesday never happened, and everybody at the table knew what it was for. He kept Lena after with the door shut. Then me: until Wednesday no argument at his table had ever sent the dog under the kitchen table. He said I went for the places that hurt, that I’m good at it, and that he’d rather I weren’t. Miss Ivors left before the goose. Nobody remembers what she was right about. Thursday he canceled the seminar for a lecture in Berkeley and gave me the week. Go. Write me something about it. Four thousand words on the second line, not one of them *liminal* — Theo’s terms; he took them. He lent me his own *Moviegoer*, his pencil in the margins. It ends on Ash Wednesday. Thirty hours in a van: he’d like to be the luggage.

s03.slug: THURSDAY · 12:15 PM · MORRO HALL 1100 — PAIR FORTY-ONE
body: The lamp in the projector clicks off on the Gulf of Mexico, and Morro 1100 comes back to itself under the fluorescent tubes, two hundred people in raked seats blinking together. The fan inside the projector keeps blowing, louder than Fenner has been all hour, cooling a slide nobody is looking at anymore: the Gulf in five blues, pale at the rim and dark in the middle, with Louisiana across the top of it like the lip of a bowl.

In row nine the kid who hummed at them on Tuesday has turned his laptop around for the row behind him, where three people are watching a boy in a Santa Cruz sweatshirt fall off a golf cart in slow motion. Fame moves on. It took two days.

Skye is beside him in the back row under the exit sign, notebook already shut, sunglasses pushed up into her hair. Out of the mouth of her bag comes a black strap and the hump of a camera he has never seen her carry, an old Nikon with the paint worn off its corners down to the brass.

Fenner unhooks his laptop at the lectern and addresses the room in the West Texas drawl that nothing, including the end of class, has ever hurried. “Pair forty-one. I’m told you’ll both be absent next week, for reasons I don’t want described.”
Every head in the hall comes around. Jack studies the fold-out desk.
“Field data,” Skye says. It carries to the front without any effort he can see. “Two oceans.”
“The Gulf’s not an ocean,” Jack says.
“Tell *it* that.”
“It’s a marginal sea, Costigan,” Fenner says, coiling his cord, “and so are you.”
The room takes its laugh with it to the doors. The projector fan goes on blowing at the blank screen.

Outside, the wind has come around out of the northwest and scoured the sky to a hard, high blue, and the glare off the lagoon brings everybody down Morro’s steps with a hand up. Past the bike racks, past the lagoon and its one egret standing in the shallows, out where the bluffs run into the Point, there is white on the water: long lines of it, one behind another, coming around the headland and bending as they come, crest after crest, like the yellow chalk on Tuesday.

Skye puts her arm through his on the top step and walks him down into the noon, her hip knocking his every second step, the camera bumping his side. Her other hand goes into his back pocket and finds a paperback where it was expecting him.
“There’s a book in here.”
“Hale’s. For the trip.”

“He put a book where I keep my hand.” She leaves the hand where it is, book and all. “*go*, with a period. I read it in his voice. Very cruel. Very attractive.” Two steps down she stops them both. “Okay. Rules for being apart. If I text you a weather report, it means I miss you.”
“What kind of weather report?”
“Any kind. Fog. Light rain. Eleven degrees, which is Canadian for not much. If I text you a *forecast*, it means I’m going to miss you later. That’s more serious. That’s missing you in advance.”
“What if it’s just the weather?”

“There’s no such thing as just the weather. I’ll be in Canada.” She takes another step. “And we’re not doing time zones. Vancouver’s on our time. You’re the one leaving it, so if you text me a forecast from a different time zone, that’s a forecast from the future, which means you already missed me, which means —” She stops on the step and works it on her fingers, lips moving, and gives up. “No. It’s broken. I built it wrong. We’re going to have to call each other like animals.”
“Where are they putting you?”
“Burnaby. It’s where Vancouver keeps the soundstages.” She frees a hand to frame it. “Burnaby has been Seattle, Oregon, two Kansases and the moon.”
“Which Kansas?”
“Both. One was a dream sequence. The moon was a miniseries, and everybody on it was very sad, and the fog machine ran for six weeks straight.”

The white iPhone comes out of her jacket. “Corinne sent notes from the network. Round two.” She reads them in Corinne’s voice: she lets all the air out of her own and keeps time with one finger. “*One. They want you less tan.*” She looks up at him over the phone. “*Two. They want a girl who has been indoors.* *Three. Please do not do anything outdoors before Friday. They have a skin person.*”
“What’s a skin person?”

“A woman in Burbank who is paid to worry about my elbows.” She scrolls. Under Corinne there is a headline, and she reads that too, with the air back in. “Oh — they’re swearing Scott Brown in *today*. A week early. That’s how you know it’s politics. Nobody in my business has been early to anything since 1974.”
“My father’s going to take it personally,” Jack says. “That was Ted Kennedy’s seat.”
“Your father takes Massachusetts personally?”
“My father takes the Kennedys personally.”
“Massachusetts sent a man in a pickup truck to fix that.”
“A GMC,” Jack says. “Pop’ll want you to know it was a GMC.”
“I’ll put it in my notes.” The phone goes back in her jacket. “What’s left on your list today?”
“Gloria.”

“Gloria,” she says, with respect, and turns around on the step above him and looks down at him from it. “Nine-thirty tonight. I’m printing. Sol said I could, for the project. She let me in in January and showed me how, one time, and now she’s in LA till Monday and I have a key and a list of things I’m not allowed to touch, which is all of them.” She pats the Nikon in its bag. “Knock first, or you’ll ruin me.”
He has walked past that door all winter: the end of Sol’s downstairs hall, shut, a red line of light along the bottom of it when somebody’s in there and nothing when they aren’t.
“That red light under the door,” he says. “I’ve been genuflecting at it since December.”
“Good instinct.” She puts a finger on the scar in his eyebrow. “Knock anyway.”
Behind her, out past the lagoon, another set comes around the Point, white along the rocks, and bends, and he watches it go the length of the headland while she watches him watch it.

response: “Counter-proposal,” he says. “If I text you a Browns score, it means I miss you.”
“It’s February.”
“That’s how you’ll know how much.”
“And if they win?”
“If the Browns win, something’s wrong with the universe. You should come home.”

She adopts it on the spot, without changing a word, and adds a clause. “Amendment. If I text you the moon, it means Burnaby’s playing it again, I’m working late, and you’re not allowed to worry.” She holds out her hand for a handshake, a firm, ridiculous, network handshake on the Morro steps, and when it’s done she keeps the hand and tows him down the last step by it, toward the lot and the Saab and the white on the water.

choices.text: *Ask her what she’s scared of about the pilot.*
response: “What are you scared of?” he says. “With the pilot.”

“Oh, I have a list.” She takes the steps one fear at a time, in descending order of glamour. “A co-star with a soul patch.” A step. “Geese. They have geese up there the size of Labradors.” A step. “Craft services. A director who calls me *kiddo*. My mother finding a direct flight.” Another. “Fog machines.”
She runs out of steps. At the bottom she stands on the walk with her sunglasses in her hand and looks at the lagoon.
“That it’s good,” she says.
She takes his arm again, harder than before, and he puts his hand over hers on his sleeve and keeps it there, and they start for the lot.
“Skip the rest,” he says. “The Point’s breaking.”
“You have a class at two.”
“I have a class at two every Thursday. The Point breaks like this twice a winter.”

She already has her keys out of the bag, the Saab key swinging on one finger, the Nikon knocking at her hip. “I was going to make you say it,” she says. “I wanted it on your conscience and not mine.” She drops the sunglasses onto her nose and starts down the walk ahead of him, backward, so she can watch him follow.
