journal.title: Oceanography 1
journal.text: Oceanography 1, Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven, Morro Hall 1100. Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Skye took it too and didn’t tell me which science till she was sitting in the back row under the exit sign with the book. Fenner: seventy-one percent, and we have better maps of Mars. The ground is not where you left it, week two. Partners by seat, Thursday. Skye, till May. No trades. Our project is the Point — why it breaks where it does. Fenner: approved, don’t drown. Tuesday: half of Pair 41. Wednesday: field data from the lot in a storm — it wasn’t breaking where it does. It was breaking everywhere. Sunday: the Point open again — breaking where it does. Saturday at the Point with Fenner’s form and a stopwatch, timing the sets. Skye called the surfers like the last hole of a golf tournament. Breaking where it does. Tuesday two hundred people had seen it. Fenner said Pair forty-one, *please*, and the room lost it. Skye was doing his refraction diagram in the margin. Thursday Fenner excused Pair 41 for next week, for reasons he doesn’t want described. Two oceans, Skye says. The Gulf is a marginal sea. So am I. Then we skipped the rest of the day for the Point, and it broke where it does, and I rode one all the way around. She shot the headland for the project on Sol’s old Nikon.

body.text: It was going to happen whoever said it. The Saab comes down the last of the dirt into the Point lot faster than the dirt would like, top up, radio off, and when Skye brakes, his Candlemas candle rolls out of the dash tray, unlit, knocks the gearshift, and rolls home again.
body.else: It was going to happen whoever said it. The Saab comes down the last of the dirt into the Point lot faster than the dirt would like, top up, radio off, and Skye brakes hard enough to put everything in the back seat into the front.

body: They had stopped at Del Playa for the boards. Tomás’s spare lives under the porch, a nine-foot log gone yellow, with masking tape across the deck: FOR EMERGENCIES. “You qualify,” Skye had said, and fed it into the back seat with its nose out his window. His two o’clock will have to get through Thursday without him; it has survived worse.

In the lot she opens both doors on her side for cover and pulls her sweater over her head, and under it she is wearing a black bikini top. She has been wearing it since eleven. She sat through Fenner in it.
“You wore that to class.”

“I had a feeling about the bottom.” She steps out of her jeans with one hand on the roof. Tomás’s spare wetsuit is on the hood for Jack, cut for a larger and more confident man, and he wrestles into it behind the open door while two spaces over a kid asleep in a hatchback goes on sleeping with his bare feet out the window. Skye gets herself into hers in the time it takes him to find one arm, then turns her back and hands him the cord. “Zip me.” He runs the zipper up her spine, his knuckles on her skin the length of it, and she shivers at the top and says, “Your hands are freezing. Good. That’s practice.”

The water is fifty-six degrees, and it says so to his feet, then his shins, and then, in one go, to everything the wetsuit was supposed to be protecting. The swell is out of the northwest, as advertised. It comes in off the open water in long dark lines, hits the rocks below the headland, and turns: each line catching on the shallows at the near end and swinging, white peeling down it toward the sand, until it is running along the Point instead of at it.

Skye goes out ahead of him on her battered shortboard, under the white water and up the other side like something that lives there. Jack goes out on nine feet of emergency. He has stood on a surfboard, in his life, for no measurable time. In December, at Ellery, the Pacific held him under until he could see his confirmation.

Outside the break it is quiet. They sit up on the boards with their legs in the water, rising and dropping, the headland above them with the old light dark on top of it. Her hair is slicked to her skull, her lips are going blue at the corners, and she is beaming.
The first wave of the next set lifts them both — a long, smooth lift under his stomach, the Pacific taking a breath — and rolls on under and away toward the rocks, bending as it goes.
“Everything bends toward the shallow end,” she tells it.
It doesn’t answer. It goes around the Point and breaks.
“Why, though?” he says. “Actually.”

“The part in the shallow water drags on the bottom and slows down. The part out in the deep keeps going. So the line swings around.” She draws it on the surface with one finger, and the ocean erases it. “Refraction. Fenner gave us the equation. I did not do the equation.” She watches the next one stand up out of the dark. “But everybody talks about it like the wave’s doing it. Like it decides to bend. It’s the bottom. The bottom’s been telling it what to do since it got here. Everybody thinks they’re the wave.”
“So what’s the bottom?”
“Depends who’s asking.” She is looking past him, out to sea. “This one. Turn around. Go. Paddle — *paddle*, Jack, you’re Catholic, you’re built for effort —”

He paddles. He feels the board picked up from behind, the tail first, the wave deciding about him, and he gets his feet under him in one long ugly scramble that Tomás would not want described — and he is up, knees bent, arms out to both sides, a scarecrow in another man’s wetsuit, and the board is going and the wave is going, and then the wave begins to turn and he turns with it, without meaning to, along the rocks, along the headland, the white curling down the line ahead of him and the green wall standing at his shoulder, past the kelp, past the place he would have bet money he’d be thrown, the noise all around him and under him and his own voice in it somewhere, yelling something with no words in it, until the wave runs out of ocean in the shallows on the inside and sets him down in two feet of water, still standing, with nothing under the board but sand.
He has ridden one around the Point. He stands in the shallows holding the board, breathing hard, and looks back up the line he came down.

Out at the top of the break Skye is sitting up on her board with both arms straight up over her head, a referee signaling a field goal, and the yell comes to him across the water a moment after he sees it.

Afterward she runs up to the Saab for the Nikon and lies down on her stomach in the dry sand, elbows planted, camera to her eye. She shoots the headland: the rocks and the white water wrapping them, the dark old light, the low wall along the top of the cliff. Her thumb works the lever after every frame.
“For Fenner,” she says, behind the camera. “He wants the bottom. I can’t photograph the bottom. So I’m photographing what it does to the top.”

Jack looks up where the lens is pointing. On the cliff the white cross stands against the wall, and on the fence wire beside it there are flowers tied on with kitchen string, white ones, going brown at the edges. He looks back at the water.

When she’s done she sets the Nikon on her towel, lens to the sky, and reaches back over her shoulder, finds the cord, and peels the wetsuit down off her arms and her shoulders and her stomach, rolling it to her hips, in February, on a public beach, with the wind out of the northwest.
“Your turn.” She is already covered in gooseflesh from her collarbones down. “To the waist. I’ll time you.”

He gets the cord, eventually, and drags the thing down. The wind hits him like a bucket of something. The St. Michael is suddenly the warmest thing on his chest and still not warm, and Skye looks at him — at the full pale length of a Youngstown winter, standing up out of a black wetsuit in broad daylight — and laughs, delighted.

“Corinne would sign you on the spot,” she says. “Look at you. You’ve been indoors since birth.” And she lays her other hand on his chest, fifty-six degrees exactly, to hear what he’ll say, and what he says is mostly a vowel.
She hooks the medal on one cold finger and lifts it off his skin. “He’s freezing,” she says, and lays him back.

There is salt drying white on her shoulders, and her hair dripping a line down her back, and a drop running from the notch of her throat down over her breastbone into the black of the bikini, and her stomach is goosebumped from her ribs to the rolled rubber at her hips, and he wants her, out here, in the afternoon, with sand stuck to both of them. It is the simplest thing he knows. She kisses him, quick, salt and cold on the outside and warm in the middle, and pulls back to look at him, and her eyes are wet from the wind.
Out past the rocks the swell is building again: a bigger set, standing up dark a long way out.
“One more,” she says, already working her arms back into her sleeves. “Then you have somewhere to be.”

response: He paddles for the biggest of the set, because it is the biggest. It lifts him higher than anything has lifted him in his life, holds him at the top to show him the view, and throws him over the front of itself, board and all. The Pacific keeps him. When it gives him back he comes up in the white water with sand in his teeth and Tomás’s leash wrapped twice around his shin.

Out at the top of the break Skye has seen all of it. She is laughing so hard she can’t stay on her own board; she slides off sideways into the water, comes up still laughing, and has to hang over the rail of it with her forehead on the wax until she can breathe.
In the Saab afterward, salt on everything, the heater going, she drives back up the dirt one-handed with the other hand on his knee, and leaves it there through every turn.
“Two-forty,” she says. “You have a woman to ask for something.”

choices.text: *Sit out past the set with her and talk.*
response: He lets the set go by under him, and she lets it go too, and in the lull after it they sit out past the break with their boards nose to nose, legs hanging in the dark water, close enough to hold each other’s rails.
“I’ve never been to Canada,” she says. “I’ve changed planes in Toronto. That doesn’t count. I’ve been to Mexico for a commercial.”
“I’ve never been south of Kentucky.”
“Jack. You’re south of Kentucky right now.”
“California doesn’t count. California’s its own direction.”
She thinks about it, bobbing. “So we’re both leaving the country,” she says. “Yours is just in the same one.”
In the Saab afterward she puts the heater on his feet, all of it, both vents turned down at his bare ankles, and drives with her own feet freezing.
“Two-forty,” she says. “You have a woman to ask for something.”

He takes the smallest wave of the set and falls off it in the most ordinary way available, and comes up, and floats on his back in the white water, and does Fenner, every vowel of West Texas he can find in an Ohio mouth. “*The specimen enters the marginal sea,*” he announces, “*and is rejected by it.*”
Skye paddles up beside him and sits up on her board to grade it. “B-minus,” she says. “For the vowels. Your Texas went through Pittsburgh.”
“Youngstown,” he says.

At the red light on the way back into town she does Fenner herself, both hands on the wheel, chin tucked, an octave down, a man who has been patient with the ocean for thirty years and is beginning to lose it. “*Pair forty-one is excused. Pair forty-one is excused from the entire hydrosphere.*” The light goes green and she doesn’t notice until somebody behind them leans on his horn.
“Two-forty,” she says, pulling away. “You have a woman to ask for something.”

s04.slug: THURSDAY · 2:40 PM · THE ANCHOR, THE COUNTER
body: In the dead hour the Anchor belongs to the pie case. The sun comes in low off the wharf and through the front glass and lays the shadow of the OPEN sign backwards across the linoleum. On the board by the pass somebody has chalked CHOWDER 4.50 and, under it, in another hand, ASK ABOUT THE FISH, which is a warning, not a special. The case, lit from inside for nobody, holds nine pies and one fly that has made up its mind about the lemon meringue. Jack still has the Point on him: salt stiff at his temples, sand in his left ear that he suspects will turn up in Texas. He has worked it out on the way over — tonight and two weeks of shifts after it, eight dollars an hour, better than three hundred before tips — and it is not a number he enjoys carrying through the door.

Up on the shelf over the register KNX is giving the news to the room. The government has opened an inquiry into the brakes on the Prius. The Colts are favored by five and a half. Dwight Freeney’s ankle gets a minute to itself, like a head of state’s. “Used to be a brake was something you pushed,” Merle says. He is the only customer, and he has been saying things to chowder since before Jack was hired. “I’ll take the Saints and the points,” he adds, unprompted.

Gloria is behind the case with a bar towel over one shoulder and a grease pencil stuck in her hair, giving each pie its quarter-turn so none of them takes the sun. She doesn’t look up for the bell over the door.
“Your roommate came in Tuesday,” she says, to the apple. “Asked me for you.”
“Gloria —”

“He had a speech. I let him finish; it had a structure. One, you’re reliable. Two, you’ve never asked anyone for anything. Three, the Saints. I asked which ones. The callback was to a pie.” The apple gets its quarter. “Then I told him it wasn’t his to ask.” She moves down the case and gives the lemon meringue the same. “Meringue, your roommate. All lift. Leave him out in the damp and he weeps.”
“I didn’t say yes till last night. I didn’t know about Tuesday —”
“Hands.” She still hasn’t turned. “You ask a woman for a thing, you stand up and say it to her face. Not to the pie.”
He is already standing. He takes his hands out of his pockets anyway, and that seems to be what she meant.

“I need tonight,” he says. “And the next two weeks, all of it. I’m going to New Orleans tomorrow, five in the morning, in a minivan, thirty hours, with five other people, and I should have called you this morning, and I’m asking now.”
Gloria turns around. She looks at him until Merle’s spoon stops: the salt, the ear, the sunburn coming up across his nose, whatever his face has been doing since September.
“There he is,” she says, to the face and not to anything he asked.
“Where was I?”
“Closing time,” Gloria says. “Since about December. What’s in New Orleans?”
“The Saints.”
“The game’s in Miami.”
“The city’s where you watch it.”
“Uh-huh,” Gloria says. Then it’s business. “Hector has tonight and the rest. He took the semester off for the baby. Six weeks old. He’ll take every hour you’ve got and ask for the ones you don’t.”
“I’ll make it up to him.”
“He’ll let you. Don’t be nice about it.” The towel comes off one shoulder and goes onto the other. “Six of you in a minivan. Somebody cries by Phoenix.”
“Tucson,” says Merle. “Everybody cries in Tucson.”
“Your professor had the back booth Saturday till close,” Gloria says. “You were off.”
“I know.”
“Told me his dog had a difficult evening, and who gave it to him.” The lemon meringue gets another eighth of a turn. It didn’t need one. “In front of the *dog*, hon?”
“What dog?” says Merle.
“Eat your chowder, Merle.”
Jack has an answer ready for the next question, who started it. Gloria goes to the register instead.

From the shelf under it she brings out the share jar, a gallon pickle jar with SHARE on a strip of masking tape, and counts his portion onto the counter in ones and fives, wetting her thumb on every fifth bill. It goes into a plain envelope. Across the front, in the grease pencil, she prints COSTIGAN, and she folds the flap down and then the envelope over twice.
“Through Sunday,” she says. “It’s early. Don’t make anything of it.”
“It’s not due till —”
“It’s due when I say.” She holds it out until he takes it. It is thicker than his share. He can tell by the weight, a week and a half in a week’s envelope, and he opens his mouth.
“Don’t count it in front of me,” Gloria says. “Count it in Texas. And don’t send me a postcard. Thirty years on my feet, I’ve been as far as Bakersfield. I don’t want to be told what it looks like.”

Back past the pass the Hobart finishes its cycle with a groan, and in the quiet Rudy speaks without turning from the sink, the rosary on his wrist swinging with the rack. He has had the date since Jack mentioned it once, over the steam, to the one man in the building who would know what to do with it.
“Your brother,” Rudy says. “The birthday.”
“He called.”
“Good.”
The Hobart starts up again. Jack puts the envelope in his shirt pocket.
“Lena’s grandmother called me this morning,” he says. “She says don’t bring anything.”
“And you believed her.”
“She’s eighty-eight.”

“That’s how you get to eighty-eight. You tell people not to bring anything and you keep count of who listened.” Gloria wipes her hands on the towel. “Since ’79 I’ve watched people carry my pies out that door. Three ways. Out in front, like an apology. Low, like a bribe. Level, both hands, like the floor’s wet and somebody’s mother is watching.” She looks at his hands. “You haven’t got a pie and you’re already carrying it level.”
“Gloria.”
“You don’t walk into somebody’s house empty-handed. I don’t care whose. Cream’s yesterday’s. Meringue weeps, you’ve met one. Apple wants a plate and a person to hold it. You pick.”

She steps aside from the case. She doesn’t do that for the other customers. She gives him all of it: the lemon meringue; the coconut cream; the apple under its lattice, his, he has been told; the boysenberry, bleeding purple into its tin; the pecan, the top gone dark and glossy and studded to the edge. Jack knows what Gloria calls the people he knows, pie by pie, and she has not been wrong yet. She isn’t watching him look. She is watching the case, the grease pencil back in her hand, giving him nothing.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew. Her granddaughter got her watching *Sweetwater*; Thursdays at nine, for the clothes. She rated Cassidy a vanilla custard. Skye agreed. Thursday I asked her for the trip. Theo asked her Tuesday; she told him it wasn’t his to ask. Hector has my shifts — the baby’s six weeks. She counted my tips out early into an envelope with my name on it in grease pencil. Hale told her about the dog. In front of the dog. She made me pick the pie for the Broussards.

journal.title: Rudy (the Anchor)
journal.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, a ballgame on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. His mother came every other Sunday — three buses from Oxnard. Says: write him, even when there’s nothing to say. I told him about Rafi’s errand like a joke. ‘I know what an errand is, mijo.’ Opened the walk-in on me Tuesday. ‘Mijo. Lettuce.’ Took the lettuce himself. Tuesday, over the Hobart: come hear my mother sing at the Mission, Saturday, five a.m. She came up from Oxnard for the Virgin and sang every verse with her eyes shut. Thursday from the dish pit: your brother, the birthday. He called. Good.

choices.key: At the Anchor you picked the Broussards’ pie: pecan. It travels — Gloria’s own words, back at her.
response: Gloria hears it come back across the counter. “Mm.”

She lifts the pecan out by its tin, sets it on a white box and brings the flaps up around it, fast, an old hand. The grease pencil comes out of her hair. On the lid, in the capitals she uses for everything in that kitchen, she writes a 5 and rings it. “Not on the floor of that van,” she says. “A pie on a floor mat has a bad trip. Somebody holds it. Somebody with a lap.” She runs the red-and-white string around twice and pulls it tight in one pull.

choices.key: At the Anchor you picked the Broussards’ pie: boysenberry. Gloria said it stains.
response: “It stains,” Gloria says. The pie is already out of its tin and onto a square of wax paper; the ones that run get wax paper.

She builds the box around it, quick and square, and looks at him once. “Mm.” Then: “Keep it off anything white. Keep it off anything you like.” On the lid she writes a 5, rings it, and parks the pencil back in her hair, behind her ear.

choices.key: At the Anchor you let Gloria pick the Broussards’ pie. She boxed the pecan without a word.
response: Gloria’s hand is on the pecan’s tin before he has finished the sentence. She boxes it with her back half turned, so that the lid is her business, and the pencil goes across it once and then round. She slides the box the length of the counter, past the napkins and the sugars, and it stops, level, against his hands.

s05.slug: THURSDAY · 4:35 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS — FRANK
body: Delgado’s front steps keep the day’s last warm stone. Jack has the third one to himself, the pie box level across his knees, the long light coming sideways through the eucalyptus, and the RAZR on the step beside him, where it is not expected to do anything. Down the walk a girl in a Pi Lam sweatshirt hauls a laundry bag toward the door by both its ears.
It goes off. The outside screen says DAD.
He lets it ring twice, out of something close to fear, and then opens it. “Pop? What’s wrong?”
“Nothing’s wrong.” On Glenwood Avenue a radio is on low, a man explaining LeBron James at some length. “Can’t I call.”
“You never call.”
“So I’m calling.”
“Where are you?”
“Garage. Truck door’s open, I got the radio.” A boot turns on concrete. “Your mother says you’re going to New Orleans.”
“Yeah.”
“For the Saints.”
“Yeah.”
“…Good.”
“I went to the bank,” Frank says. “Market Street. There’s sixty dollars in your account. For gas.”

Sixty dollars is gas for the Silverado to Pittsburgh and back twice. Jack does the sum before he can stop himself, and he’d bet the sixty his father did it first, at the window, with somebody watching.
“Pop —”
“Sixty. A hundred’s showing off.”
“Pop. With everything, you can’t just —”
“Cruze line, next year,” Frank says. “Maybe.” The radio goes to a mattress commercial. “It ain’t a question.”
“The girl at the window said that was a nice thing to do for somebody.” The boot again. “I told her it’s gas.”
Against his chest, in the shirt pocket, the Anchor’s envelope. Two people have counted money out for him today, and neither would let him watch.
“Your roommate e-mailed your mother a budget.”
“Theo did?”
“Dear Mrs. Costigan. With a chart. A pie chart.” Frank gives that its due. “I said what’s the pie. Your mother said it’s a kind of graph. Gas, forty-one percent. Food. A slice called Contingency.”
“What’s Contingency?”

“Your mother says it’s for if he’s wrong. Down the bottom it says Yours in transit. I said what’s that. She said it’s how rich people sign.” Something clinks onto the bench. “Sixty-one dollars a head. She printed it. It’s on the refrigerator under St. Joseph.”
“Pop —”
“Sixty is a number,” Frank says. “Sixty-one is a man who rounded up. The kid said sixty-one. You find the dollar.”

body.text: “Your grandmother’s telling the whole Altar Society the TV one’s got range. I don’t know what that means and I’m not asking.”
“It means she’s good, Pop.”
“Huh,” Frank says.

body: “Hold on.” Paper rustles on the bench, folded small. “Your mother wrote it down.”

“Gina wants footage. I said he don’t have the camera. She said he has a phone. I said that phone’s no good for it.” The paper again. “Rosie wants the crabs. A report. She gave your mother a list in Latin, I’m not reading it.”
“Callinectes sapidus.”

“That.” Frank does not sound sorry he asked. “Your mother lit the St. Joseph candle in the kitchen for the trip. I said it’s a car, not a war. She said St. Joseph doesn’t know the difference and neither does she.” The paper goes back into a pocket. “That was hers. The rest is me.”
“What is it, a Honda?”
“An Odyssey. It’s Kevin’s mother’s.”
“Honda makes a motor. Have him check the oil at the Arizona line. Who’s driving?”
“Kevin first. Then me, through Texas.”
“Kevin any good?”
“He’s pre-med. He drives like there’s a patient in the back.”
“That’s a driver. Texas is the long one. You remember Nebraska.”
“Pop, I remember Nebraska.”
“You get tired, you pull over before you think you have to. Sleeping’s free. I checked.”
“Okay.”
“What’s it down there, sixty?”
“Sixty-two, they said.”
“In February.” Frank lets that go by. “Here it’s nine.”
“Colts by five and a half, they say.”
“They say.” Frank has opinions about this. “Manning I don’t like. Man changes the play at the line. A play’s a play. You call it, you run it.”
“He’s good at it, Pop.”
“That’s what I don’t like. You watching it down there?”
“Sunday. Yeah.”
“Watch it with people. That’s the whole thing. You don’t watch it by yourself.”
“I won’t.”
“And you look at the river. The Mississippi. I never saw that one. I saw the —” He clears his throat. “The Pacific. It was big. I looked at it a while. It’s allowed.”
“Okay, Pop.”
“And tell the TV one your mother says Canada’s cold.”

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.” Asked me what it’s like in there. Went in on Holy Family Sunday — his name was on the list at the desk; he asked Ma where he’s supposed to stand. Told Danny about the hall and the Cruze, and laughed, in there. Asked if the Saints girl sent the coffee. I said yeah. Told Danny they wouldn’t lose. Three straight. His phone died in the cold and he borrowed mine. New Year’s: a ginger ale, in a glass. New Year’s: two spoons of lentils, for the money. “Pryor.” Went in to see Danny again. “Four straight.” Twelfth Night we took the lights down, and the beer fridge is ginger ale now. At the curb in Pittsburgh: call your mother when you land. She don’t sleep. Thursday he called me — him, not Ma. He put sixty dollars in my account for gas. It ain’t a question. Theo e-mailed Ma a budget, with a chart. Watch it with people, he says; that’s the whole thing. Tell the TV one Ma says Canada’s cold.

choices.key: Your father put sixty dollars in your account for gas. You said thanks, Pop. He said yeah.
response: “Yeah.”
“Your mother wants to know did you eat. I’m not asking.”
“I ate.”
The radio goes on with its business. “I’ll tell her you said so.”

choices.key: Your father put sixty dollars in your account for gas. You told him to put it on Danny’s books instead. He left yours where it was.
response: A can goes down on the workbench, hard enough to ring. “Your brother’s got money,” Frank says. The radio fills the space where the rest of it would go. “Your brother’s got more money than you.”
The sixty stays in Jack’s account. When he says goodnight he says, “Your brother’s books are my business,” and that’s all of it.

choices.text: “I’ve got it, Pop. I’ve got tips.”
choices.key: Your father put sixty dollars in your account for gas. You told him you’ve got tips. It ain’t a question, he said — twice.
response: “It ain’t a question.” Flatter this time, and final. “Keep the tips for the way home.”
The truck door thunks shut at his end, close to the phone, and the radio goes small behind the glass.

s05a.slug: THURSDAY · 5:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS — TWO TEXTS
body: The RAZR is still warm from Ohio when it goes off again in his hand, twice, close together.

body.text: three suitcases. a crisis. come watch me fail
412. The labeled bags have arrived. Come and witness.

body: Skye’s has three suitcases in it and no capitals: by her standards, a distress flare. Theo’s is punctuated like a telegram from a duke.

The sun is down in the tops of the eucalyptus, and the light comes long and orange across the steps and over the pie box on his knees, and the bikes in the rack lay their shadows halfway to the road. Kevin won’t open his mother’s van for loading till eight. That leaves the better part of three hours, a pie, and two people who have each, in their own way, asked him to come and look at luggage.

s06s.slug: THURSDAY · 5:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THREE SUITCASES
body: Tomás is grinding coffee again, at suppertime, for reasons of his own. It comes up through the floor of her room in long ratcheting bursts, stops, starts again, and behind the house the surf is breaking at the bottom of the bluff, and in the window over the bed the sun has just gone into the Pacific and left it red.

Three suitcases lie open: one on the mattress, one on the floor, one on the desk chair with its lid tipped back against the wall. The clothes rack in the corner is down to bare hangers at one end. On the dresser, propped against the jar of beach glass, her white iPhone lies face-up on speaker, and Corinne is coming out of it from a car somewhere in Los Angeles with every consonant filed to a point.
“The skin person called me,” Corinne says. “She wants to know if you went outside today.”
Skye is on her knees beside the suitcase on the floor, her hair still stiff from the Point and a line of dried salt along her jaw. “No,” she says.
“Because they were very specific. A girl who’s been *indoors*.”
“Mm.”

Behind the phone’s back, for Jack in the doorway, she becomes the girl. She shrinks from the desk lamp with a forearm over her eyes. She sags by stages down the side of the suitcase, a houseplant somebody forgot in a closet, and comes to rest face-down in a pile of sweaters with one hand still raised so Corinne will know she’s listening.

“Car meets you in Vancouver. The sign won’t have your name on it, it’ll have the character’s, so look for *Cassie*. Wardrobe at two. And Skye. It’s two weeks. You’re furniture with lines. Be furniture.”
“Kay.”
“Text me from the gate.”
“Bye, Corinne.” She reaches back without looking and ends the call with her elbow.
She lifts her face out of the sweaters. “Three suitcases. It’s a crisis. I told you.”
“You said you’d fail.”

“I’m failing. Look at me.” She points without getting up. “That one’s Cassie. Cassie has been indoors. Cassie owns four cardigans and a feeling about her father. That one’s me. And that one’s the rain, because I looked it up, and Vancouver in February is the inside of a cloud with a Starbucks in it.”

The one on the bed won’t shut. She gets up and sits on it, and it still won’t, so he sits on it with her, side by side on Cassie’s cardigans with their knees touching, and she bounces once, businesslike, and the latch catches.
“Teamwork.” She keeps her seat, leaning on him, her shoulder under his arm; her hair smells like the Point. “Get my passport. Drawer under the glass. I can’t get up. If I get up, Cassie gets out.”

The drawer sticks and comes. Under a snarl of chargers and a roll of film in its canister, the passport is there, navy blue, the eagle on the cover worn soft at the corners from being carried. He opens it.

The girl in the picture is sixteen. Her braces have just come off — he can tell from the way she holds her mouth, still guarding them — and her hair is dyed a flat drugstore brown for some part he’ll have to ask about. Beside her face the government has typed her name in its block letters, as it would anybody’s.
He reads it off the page. “Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle.”
On the suitcase she holds still. She has her hands in her lap, and she watches his mouth while he says it.
“It’s the only one that calls me that,” she says.
He has known the name a week. It looks different with an eagle on it. He’s still looking when she holds out her hand.
“Give it here. The Department of State has been very formal with me for three years. I don’t want you getting ideas.” She sets it on the dresser beside the phone, lined up with the edge.

His flannel is over the back of the desk chair, where it has lived since January, the salsa still on the cuff. She shakes it out, folds it in a way it would hurt Theo to watch, and lays it on top in the suitcase on the floor.
“That’s mine,” Jack says.
“It’s coming. It has a part.”
“What part?”

“Small. Recurring. It doesn’t say anything. It just turns up in scenes, and everybody knows what it means.” She pats it down. “On your way out, don’t open the door at the end of the hall. My afternoon’s in there drying.”
“The Point?”
“The Point. The rocks. Some surfer.” She pats the flannel again. “Don’t open it.”

Out of the lid pocket of the suitcase on the chair she pulls a few stapled pages, folded the long way and gone furry along the fold, and holds them out. PORT ALDER, it says across the top, and under that, *“Pilot” — Scene 14 — EXT. THE PORCH — NIGHT.* The girl’s lines are gone over in yellow highlighter. The other part is pink.
“Read with me.”
“Who’s pink?”

“Wade. Her father. He’s been gone fifteen years, and tonight he comes up the porch steps with a duffel bag and no explanation, which is a very strong choice for a man on network television.” She stands up in the middle of the rug in her socks. “Just read it. Don’t act. I can’t stand it when people act at me in my bedroom.”
He reads it. “Hi, kid.”

It comes out like a man reading the back of a cereal box, and it doesn’t slow her down. She’s already gone. She stands with her arms folded across herself, nineteen and furious, on a porch in a town that doesn’t exist, and looks at the place where Wade would be: Jack.
“It’s Cassie,” she says. “It’s been Cassie for a while.”
He finds the next pink. “You got tall.”
“I got fifteen years. Tall came with them.”
“I wrote you.”
“Twice. I have them both. I know what they say better than you do.” She takes a step toward a screen door that isn’t there. “I heard the truck, you know. That morning. I thought you forgot your —”

The line quits on her halfway. In the same motion she drops straight down, sitting, into the open suitcase on the floor, knees up, his flannel under her, and pulls the lid down over herself to the chin, a girl being packed for shipment, and says from inside it, in Corinne’s filed consonants, “Be furniture.”
Jack stands in the middle of her room with Wade’s page in his hand. He saw where it quit. He keeps his thumb on the place.
Downstairs, the grinder starts up again.

response: He reads it again, slower. “Hi, kid.” He gives it the porch steps first, and the duffel, and fifteen years of working up to it in a truck, and says it as Wade might, if he weren’t sure he was allowed to.

She climbs out of the suitcase. She finds her mark on the rug and folds her arms and starts again from *It’s Cassie*, and when she comes to the truck she goes through it — “I thought you forgot your thermos. I went to the window. I waited up for a *thermos*, Wade” — and on to the bottom of the page, where the writers have Cassie shut the screen door on him. She shuts it, on nothing, quietly.
Afterward she doesn’t look at him. She goes to the dresser, puts the passport back in the drawer under the jar of glass, and slides it shut.
“Seven-fifty,” she says, with her hand still on the drawer. “Go put things in a van. Nine-thirty. Knock.”
“Hi, kid,” he says, in Glenwood Avenue — flat, from the chest, with a pause after it you could park the Silverado in. Wade adds, off the page: “Close your mouth. You’ll catch flies.”
The suitcase shakes.
“Again,” she says from inside it. “Louder. At the floor. Tomás has to hear this.”
So he gets down on his knees on her rug and says it into the floorboards, and downstairs the grinder stops mid-bean and doesn’t start again.

Her phone lights up on the dresser: CORINNE. She answers it on speaker with one finger, without picking it up — “Mm-hm” — and steers him to the door with her free hand in the middle of his back. “Seven-fifty. Go put things in a van. Nine-thirty. Knock.”
Behind them on the dresser Corinne is still talking, filing the edges off the word *Burnaby*, to a girl who is laughing at something else.
“You went somewhere on that line,” he says.
She looks up at him over the lid. “Professional secret.”
She climbs out, kneels, and brings the lid down over his flannel, fast, and her own fingers are still on the rim when it lands. He sees her leave them there.
She swears at the suitcase, low, and shakes the hand out and puts a knuckle in her mouth, and he looks at the hand and not at her face, and she seems to want it that way.
“Seven-fifty,” she says, and runs the zipper around three sides, over the flannel, and pats the top. “Go put things in a van. Nine-thirty. Knock.”

s06t.slug: THURSDAY · 5:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — MEDIUM SPARKLE
body: The speakers on Theo’s sill are already going when Jack gets the door open with his elbow, the pie box out in front of him in both hands: a piano that finds one chord and keeps going back to it, patient as somebody knocking at a house with the lights on, and under it a drum machine that has all night. The sun is down in the eucalyptus. What is left of it comes through the one window and lies across 412 in a long orange slab, and in the slab, side by side on the two made beds, sit two bags.

They are quilted, pink and enormous, with grosgrain bows on the handles that look measured. Across the flap of each, on a strip of white label-maker tape, is a name. Theo’s says MR. THEODORE, MEDIUM SPARKLE. Jack’s says FIREMAN, LARGE.
Theo stands at the foot of the beds in his shirtsleeves with his hands clasped behind him, as at a viewing.
“Close the door,” he says. “And witness.”
Jack closes it with his heel and sets the pie on his desk, beside the mug.
“Is that Gloria’s?” Theo asks.
“She says you came in Tuesday and asked for me.”
“I consulted her.”
“She says it wasn’t yours to ask.”
“I’ve been replaying it,” Theo says. “She didn’t even look up from the pie case. It was the finest no I have ever been given, and I was once refused a table at the Polo Lounge in front of my father.”
“Who brought them up?”

“Marcus, on the move-in cart. I didn’t ask what she paid him. I’m guessing a casserole and a look. She was up till two with the label maker.” He tilts his head at the floor. “I heard it through two floors. A very small typewriter that has been wronged.” His own bag sits untouched, with a kind of clearing around it. “I said I wouldn’t open it alone. A man shouldn’t be alone with a bag that knows his soul.”

He unzips it and takes out the first thing his hand finds: a black Saints T-shirt sequined from collar to hem in gold. It catches what is left of the window and throws it across the ceiling in a thousand small coins.
“Sequins,” Jack says.
“‘Medium,’” says Theo. “She was being modest.”

Under the shirt there is a hank of Mardi Gras beads in purple, green and gold, wound up like fishing line, and under that, folded in tissue as if it were evening wear, a black satin sleep mask. Theo lifts the mask out in both hands and holds it to the light.
“She knows my soul,” he says, quietly.

He puts the beads on, and the shirt on over the one he is wearing, and turns a slow circle in the slab of light. The coins go around the room: over both beds, over the crucifix, over Jack by the desk, and for a few seconds 412 is a ballroom at the end of a very long party.
“You look like a bowling trophy,” Jack says.

“A bowling trophy that has been told it can stay up late.” Theo stops with his arms a little out from his sides and looks down at the front of himself. “It’s the only thing I own that has ever been enthusiastic on my behalf.” He peels the shirt off over his head, carefully, so as not to lose a sequin, and the beads after it, and lays them on the bed.

Jack opens FIREMAN, LARGE, and it is a different kind of document. Foam earplugs, sealed in pairs. An inflatable horseshoe pillow with its valve taped shut. A box of Dramamine. Three packs of gum in three flavors, as if flavor were an insurance policy. And an extra-large Saints T-shirt, plain black cotton, the fleur-de-lis printed flat, not a sequin on it anywhere.
“She spared you the sparkle,” Theo says. “Don’t mistake that for mercy. That’s tailoring.”
“Dramamine. I don’t get carsick.”
“She’s provided for your worst day, Costigan. Be moved.”
An index card is tucked into the pillow’s fold, written in a round hand that makes every period a small balloon.

body.title: An index card, inside the bag
body.text: 30 HRS. BEHAVE. —D.

body: Under the D there is a flourish you could hang a banner from.
“D,” Jack says.

“For Delaney. It’s how she signs a warning.” Theo folds the mask back into its tissue and lifts the tissue to check under it, and then checks the bag. “Mine has no card. Yours has instructions. Mine has faith.” He sets the mask on the bed beside the shirt. “She sized you from the Commons steps with one eye shut and her thumb up, like a painter. I was asked to confirm. I confirmed.”

Jack’s own packing takes four minutes: the duffel from Glenwood Avenue, jeans, a week of socks that he suspects is optimistic, the rosary. Hale’s *Moviegoer* is already where it has been since this morning, in his back pocket. Theo’s takes the evening. The weekender lies open on the floor, camel leather with TAV across the flap in letters you could sign a treaty with, and he builds into it in ranks: shirts rolled and laid out by their likelihood of creasing, socks balled and sorted by temperament, the blazer folded in thirds with tissue in the lapels, Ma’s scarf in a place of honor in case New Orleans takes a turn, the sequins set apart in a pillowcase of their own, in quarantine.
“It’s a weekend bag,” Jack says.
“It’s a bag with sequins in it. The sequins snag the wool, the wool pills the satin, and the beads have a grievance against everything. I have seated weddings with fewer landmines.”
On the nightstand Hollis sits in his teacup with a laminated card propped against the saucer in Priya Raman’s hand: CUSTODIAN: P. RAMAN, R.A. TERMS ATTACHED.

body.text: “You told me I’d never asked you for anything,” Theo says, to a sock. “I’ve been trying to decide all day if that was a compliment.” Jack starts to answer and is waved off with the sock.

body: “I didn’t thank you,” Theo says, with his back to Jack, folding. “For the text.”
“You asked.”
“I’m aware. I’m told it’s habit-forming.”

He folds a sock into its partner and looks at the result. “That call,” he says. “In January. When you were home.” The sock goes into the weekender with great care. “She asked would you be around after, and you said you had a thing. What was the thing?”
“Theo.”
“Hypothetically.”
“It’s done,” Jack says. “Fold your socks.”
Theo folds his socks.
“How’s Callender?” he asks, between one sock and the next.
“Three suitcases and a crisis. I’m seeing her at nine-thirty.”
“Naturally.”

Theo takes the shirt he folded a minute ago out of the weekender, shakes it open, and folds it again: sleeves back, then in thirds, then once more than that. The piano goes around to its second chord and the drum machine comes in under it. Down the hall a rolling suitcase finds every seam in the linoleum, and a door opens on somebody else’s weekend. Behind Jack, FIREMAN, LARGE sits open with its horseshoe pillow out, and Theo, on his knees on the floor, smooths the shirt flat on his thigh and does not put it in.

response: Theo stops. The shirt stays where it is.

“Don’t thank me,” he says. “Not for this one.” And he puts it in the weekender, on top of the pillowcase of sequins. He has spent the evening ruling out exactly that arrangement. He closes the flap on it.

The bag was finished at six. It takes Theo until five to eight to agree: by seven the window is black and the first lamp is on in the lot, and at half past he discovers that the beads belong on the outside of the weekender, and the ranks have to be redone around them. Then he hands Jack FIREMAN, LARGE by its bows and reaches over and cuts the speaker in the middle of a bar, and the piano stops on a note, and the room has to hold its shape without it.

choices.text: *Put on the sleep mask and critique his folding.*
response: Jack lifts the mask out of its tissue while Theo is still too surprised to stop him, and pulls it down over his eyes. It is cool and slick and smells of Laney’s hand cream, gardenia, a Texas threat.
“The sleeves are amateur,” he says to the dark, and to roughly where Theo was. “The collar’s facing the wrong wall. I’m told there are socks, and I can only assume it’s a disaster.”
Theo laughs outright, and then, because he cannot help it, pitches it. “A blind man reviews a weekender. Rated R for linens. It’s an awards picture, Costigan. It opens in December.”

Jack keeps the mask on through the rest of the folding, on principle, issuing notes. At five to eight Theo’s hand finds the light switch and the room goes dark, and Jack, in satin, is the last person in it to find out. “We’re going down,” Theo says, and puts FIREMAN, LARGE into his hands by its bows.

choices.text: “Why do you need me there, Theo?”
response: Theo stops with a sock in each hand. “Because I asked,” he says.
He becomes absorbed in the weekender’s luggage tag. He reads it front and back, though there is nothing on it but his name. Theo does not fill the quiet, and they finish the bag in it.
At five to eight the mask goes into his blazer pocket, not the bag, where he can reach it. He lifts FIREMAN, LARGE off the bed and holds it out to Jack by its bows.

s07.slug: THURSDAY · 8:00 PM · THE ANACAPA LOT — THE ODYSSEY
body: The sodium lamps over the Anacapa lot turn everything the same burnt orange: the peeling eucalyptus along the far edge, the parking stripes, the bike cage, and Kevin’s mother’s Honda Odyssey, whatever color it is by day. It is backed into its space under the window of 420 with the hatch up and the dome light on. The La Vang rosary hangs from the mirror. The TRAN first-aid kit is strapped to the back of the passenger seat with two bungee cords, one more than it has ever needed. The cooler waits on the asphalt behind the bumper. Out of the open hatch, at a volume a mother would sign off on, comes the first of the two Carpenters songs on Kevin’s *Road Trip Mix*.

Kevin is at the driver’s door in his quarter-zip, holding a clipboard against his chest like a chart at a bedside. Taped to the dash at all four corners is a seating chart Jack can’t read from the back of the van. Beside it, taped the same way, is a new index card in Kevin’s block capitals.

body.title: Taped to the dash, beside the chart
body.text: SPEED: 65. NOT 66. · OIL AT THE AZ LINE. · GAS AT HALF A TANK, NOT A QUARTER. · RECEIPTS TO LENA.

body: Somewhere on Glenwood Avenue, Frank Costigan has been beaten to the oil by a pre-med.

Kevin has a second sheet, folded in quarters. He leans across the passenger seat, puts it in the glovebox and goes back to his clipboard, and Theo, passing the open door with his weekender, gives the glovebox two pats until it clicks shut, and keeps walking.

body.text: Jack has come up from Del Playa by way of 412 at something close to a jog, with the duffel over his shoulder and Gloria’s pie in both hands, level. Laney is at the back of the van sorting a row of pink quilted bags along the bumper, bows on the handles, a strip of label-maker tape across every flap. She peels off the one marked FIREMAN, LARGE and holds it out to him without looking at him. “You missed the unveiling.”
body.else: Jack has come down the stairs behind Theo with the duffel on one shoulder and FIREMAN, LARGE on the other, the label tape already lifting at one corner, and Gloria’s pie in both hands, level. Laney is at the back of the van sorting a row of pink quilted bags along the bumper, bows on the handles. She sees her bag on him and goes on sorting.

body: Clare Dominguez is here in her 49ers cap, with a steel thermos she gives to Kevin as soon as he has a hand free. While he is still holding it she leans in past him and wedges a holy card into the driver’s visor: Our Lady of La Vang in a gold áo dài, the Child on her arm. “For the roads,” Clare says. “It’s coffee in there. It’s strong. Don’t let Theo have any.”
“Slander,” says Theo, from inside the van.

At five past eight the side door of Delgado lets Lena out. Jack has the cooler by both handles, halfway up to the bumper, and what he gets of her is what comes in at the edge of things: one bag on a shoulder, a cardboard box riding a hip, boots on the asphalt. He doesn’t raise his head. She doesn’t look over. She sets the box down by the back tire and speaks to Kevin, at Jack’s elbow.
“Kevin, the cooler goes in last.”
Kevin, to Jack, who is holding the cooler: “The cooler goes in last.”
“I heard,” Jack says, to Kevin.
“He heard,” Kevin says, and writes it on the clipboard.

Jack puts the cooler back down where it was. Lena takes a yellow legal pad out of her bag and uncaps a pen. It is a parking lot and a van, and she is somebody with an opinion about a cooler, and he has a duffel that needs a place to go, and at that size it suits him fine.

It runs that way from there. The bench in the way-back folds forward, Lena tells Kevin, and the soft bags go under it. Kevin says so to Jack. Jack wants to know whether a duffel counts as soft, and asks Kevin, and Kevin turns around and asks the hatch, where Lena is writing on the pad, and the answer comes back by the same route, Lena to Kevin to Jack. Duffels are soft.

“I’m pre-med,” Kevin says, setting the second of Laney’s three suitcases in on its side. “I’m not a switchboard.” He looks at the third, still waiting on the asphalt. “Three suitcases for two weeks is a presentation, Laney. I’d want to run tests.”
“Laney.” Lena’s pen keeps moving. “Would you let him know the bench is a seat. Bags go under it, not on it. People are going to sit there for thirty hours.”
“I am not *Western Union*, Lena.”

Laney turns around anyway and delivers it to Jack, every word, in a voice like a frost advisory for the higher elevations. “The bench is a seat. Bags go under it. Not on it. People are going to sit there for thirty hours.”
Jack takes his duffel off the bench and puts it on the asphalt.
“And that’s the last free one,” Laney says, to everybody. “Anybody else needs a thing said, I charge by the syllable, and y’all know I’m not cheap.”
Theo puts his head out of the side door. “Kevin, tell Lena that if we’re assigning the floor —”
“No,” Kevin says.

The head withdraws. A minute later Theo tries the lot at large, one hand up to frame it. “Picture it. Six friends. One minivan. Nineteen hundred miles of open road, and at the end of it a city that has waited forty-three years for —” Not one of them looks up. He lets the rest of the sentence walk off across the asphalt by itself and gets very busy with Margot’s milk crate.

Margot is sitting sideways in the open side door with her Docs on the running board and the crate at her feet: Interstate 10 printed out county by county in three colors of highlighter, and a Radio Shack tape recorder with its red light on. “Field season,” she says, when Jack looks at the light. “I closed the archive last night. Seven versions. In the seventh the dog gives an interview.”

Four floors up, the window of 420 scrapes open, and Doug Pruitt leans out of it in silhouette with something between his fingers that glows when he breathes in. “COSTIGAN.” He waits for the lot to look up, and the lot does. “IS THE DOG GOING?”
“Nobody answer him,” Kevin says.
The lot goes on loading. Laney reorganizes a bag she has already organized. Theo reads the label on the first-aid kit. Margot’s red light takes it all down, and in time the window scrapes shut.

Kevin comes past with the third of Laney’s suitcases, beaming at both ends of the van. “Fun fact,” he says. “I’m going to spend my life telling people things they don’t want to hear, in rooms they can’t leave. I really thought I’d get to start in a hospital.” The smile holds. He puts the suitcase in.
When Jack brings his money over, Kevin has the treasurer’s binder clip out and doesn’t reach for it. “Your share’s paid.”
“By who?”
Kevin looks at Theo. Theo is reading the first-aid kit again.

Jack takes out Gloria’s envelope, COSTIGAN across the front in grease pencil, and counts it into Kevin’s palm under the dome light, in the Anchor’s ones and fives, gone soft in the share jar: fives up to fifty-five, then ones, and the sixty-first is a single with somebody’s phone number on it in ballpoint. Kevin regards the money in his hand. He pulls three twenties and a one out of the binder clip and holds them out sideways, and Theo takes his own money back and puts it inside his blazer without a word.
At the hatch Lena writes something on the pad. She doesn’t look up.
At twenty past eight Clare has a rehearsal. She tugs the brim of the cap at the van in general and says to Kevin, “Call me from Texas.”
“I will.”

She heads off across the lot toward the music building with her hands in her peacoat. Kevin watches her as far as the bike cage with his big easy smile on, the one that never quite reaches his eyes, and then he looks down at the clipboard and turns a page.
The pie comes next. “It can’t ride in cargo,” Kevin says. “Not on the floor.”
“Kevin, sugar, if you say *cargo* one more time tonight I will load you,” Laney says. “Not on the floor.”
“A pie on a floor mat,” Theo says. “Gila Bend. They find the box in the morning. It’s a horror picture.”
Margot holds out both arms. “Give it to me. For science.”

Jack gives it to her. She settles it across her knees in the side door with Gloria’s five, ringed in grease pencil, faced up into the dome light, and lays both hands on the lid. “It sleeps in 305,” she says. “I’ll be up.”

At the hatch Laney and Theo pass each other, an armload each, and on the way by a folded yellow sheet goes from his hand into hers. Laney puts it in her bra. Theo looks up at the stars, of which the Anacapa lot has three, one of them a plane.

Margot hasn’t taken her hands off the pie. “In some societies,” she says, “a man may not speak to his mother-in-law. Everything goes through a third party. Radcliffe-Brown called it an *avoidance relationship*.”
“Margot,” says Laney. “*Hush.*”
Margot looks down at the red light on her recorder, and switches it off, and doesn’t switch it back on.
Theo reaches into the front and turns the Carpenters up a notch. No one stops him.
That leaves the seats. Kevin lifts the clipboard to start on them, and two people speak to him at once from opposite ends of the van.
“Kevin, I’ll take the way-back,” Lena says.
“Kevin, I’ll take the way-back,” Jack says.
Kevin closes his eyes. “There’s one way-back.”
“It seats three,” says Margot.
“No it does *not*,” says Laney.

body.text: Theo finds something urgent to do with the zipper on his weekender.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the fundraiser: a room raised for a cause, handed to its opposition. Skye said she didn’t hand them the room, she introduced them to me, and she’s still voting for Boxer. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Four versions of Wednesday are going around Delgado, she says. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture. Monday night in the Fishbowl: six versions of Wednesday now. One has reached the Classics department. She wouldn’t read me any of them. Thursday night at the van she took the pie on her lap, for science, and told the van about men in some societies who may not speak to their mothers-in-law; everything goes through a third party. Radcliffe-Brown. Then she turned her recorder off.

journal.title: Clare Dominguez
journal.text: Clare Dominguez. Newman sophomore. Plays violin in the Mass band. Played ‘Ashokan Farewell’ at the Haiti table and people stopped on the lawn. Kevin’s mother knows her mother. Everybody’s mother knows her mother. Four brothers, back in San Jose. Knows football better than Kevin. Wore a 49ers cap to Sully’s. At the Walk for Life a man with a megaphone screamed at her, and she kept praying. Skye stood in front of her. Thursday at eight she came to the lot with a thermos for Kevin and a holy card of Our Lady of La Vang. Call me from Texas. She left at twenty past.

response: Kevin opens his eyes. “God bless you,” he says, with feeling, and leans through the open door and taps the chart on the dash. “Middle captain’s chair, right side. Your back to the way-back. Which is where I put you in the first place.”

He runs his finger down it so everyone can see: Kevin at the wheel; Theo riding shotgun, labeled THE PRODUCER; Margot middle left; Jack middle right; and in the way-back, Laney on the right and Lena on the left, behind Margot. “It’s been final since before anybody asked me,” Kevin says, and pulls his head back out of the van.

choices.text: “Tell her I called the way-back in 2009.”
response: Kevin looks at Laney. Laney sighs from the bottom of her boots and relays it to the hatch word for word. “He called the way-back in 2009.”
Lena, to Laney, with the pen still going: “Tell him it’s 2010.”
Laney turns back to Jack. “It’s 2010.”

“Thank you both,” Kevin says. He holds the clipboard up at arm’s length like an eye chart, and on it is the same chart that’s taped to the dash, drawn before anybody asked him: Kevin at the wheel; Theo riding shotgun, labeled THE PRODUCER; Margot middle left; Jack middle right; Laney and Lena in the way-back, Lena on the left, behind Margot. “Read me the bottom line,” Kevin says. From where Jack stands it reads fine.

choices.text: “Put me as far from the way-back as the car goes.”
response: Kevin, very quietly: “That’s the hood.”
At the hatch a strap is pulled tight, hard, the buckle ratcheting. Jack doesn’t turn.

Kevin doesn’t lift the clipboard. He just points, one seat at a time, the chart he drew in the first place: himself at the wheel; Theo up front; Margot middle left; Jack middle right, his back to the way-back; and in the way-back, Laney, and on the left, behind Margot, Lena. He keeps the finger up until everyone has seen where it went.

s07a.slug: THURSDAY · 8:40 PM · THE ANACAPA LOT — THE BOX FROM OAKLAND
body: The box is the last thing left on the asphalt. Somebody packed it with care: brown paper over the cardboard, the corners folded hospital-tight, twine both ways and knotted on top, and across the lid in a careful upright hand, FOR MRS. BROUSSARD. In the corner, smaller, a return address: J. PARK-ELLIS, and a street in Oakland.
“Where does Julian go?” Kevin says.
“On top of the cooler,” says Margot, from behind the pie.
Kevin sets it on top of the cooler at the hatch end, lined up with the edges, and steps back from it. In Margot’s crate the recorder sits with its red light off.

Kevin goes around to the passenger side, opens the glovebox himself, takes out a little white bottle with a sponge tip, shuts the glovebox again, and walks the bottle back to the hatch and holds it out to Lena. Kevin says nothing. She takes it.

Jack is in the back on one knee, working the duffel in under the way-back bench where duffels go. Over his head the hatch light is on, and the raised glass is getting letters. They come a stroke at a time, white, on the outside, so that from underneath he gets them backward: WHO DAT · 3 DAYS.
He knows the hand. He puts the duffel in.
Lena is at the open hatch now, white on two of her fingers, both hands on the cargo strap across the bags, taking up the slack.

When he backs out, Laney points him with her chin at the last of her luggage, a quilted train case the size of a tackle box still sitting by Delgado’s side door. He goes and gets it. It is heavier than anything a train case has a right to be, and something inside it clinks.

Theo has walked off to the edge of the lot, past the bike cage where the orange gives out, with his phone to his ear. Coming back past him with the train case, Jack finds him half turned away with his free hand clamped on top of his head.
“…No. Don’t go in the pool house. Mom. Leave it. I’ll — leave it.”

Theo sees him. He tips the phone away from his mouth. “Sandbags,” he says, and smiles. “They’re saying rain Friday night. The hill behind her house.” The phone goes back to his ear. “Mom. I’m here. I’m listening.”
Jack carries the train case on to the van.

Laney takes it from him at the side door, in the quilted vest and a black-and-gold beanie with a pompom that has no idea what kind of night it is, and stows it under her own seat with her own hands. She has an index card out and is going down it with a Sharpie, ticking as she goes: bags, six; train case; pillows, six; snacks, salty; snacks, sweet; Kevin’s coffee, with DO NOT TOUCH beside it and, in smaller capitals, THEO. She ticks the train case. She keeps hold of the door frame and says one more thing to him, low, and this one doesn’t come through anybody:
“That’s from Julian. For her mama. He’s not coming, if you were wondering. He told her, *It’s your city. I’d be a tourist in it. Go.*”
He’s annoyed, and more annoyed that it shows. A month of *Jack* with nothing on it, and now she wants to watch his face.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. The Advent party: plays piano too, by ear. Under contraband mistletoe he kissed her cheek. Kissed her goodbye at his car, for Oakland. Asked me to make sure she eats before her flight. In sixty-one pictures from Lucille’s baptism, at the Broussards’ table between Mémère and Josie. Tess’s caption calls him *le petit violon*. Flew home to Oakland on the fourth. Tuesday morning, on the feed: a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late; Lena tagged. Songs for Haiti, Friday at Bastille, every dollar to CRS. Theo asked him how many are about her. ‘One.’ At Sully’s Lena introduced him to Skye. ‘The flyers.’ Theo says the new one is about a river. Monday he was at the foot of the Hollis stairs with her bag on his shoulder. He held the door for her, and then for me. He sent a box from Oakland for Mrs. Broussard. He isn’t coming. It’s her city, he told her; he’d be a tourist in it. Laney made sure I heard.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Monday night she and Theo were on the lounge floor with two legal pads side by side, and turned them over when I came in. A wedding seating chart, Theo said. Hypothetical. She took ink off my face with her thumb, and went cold again. Thursday night at the van she said she wasn’t Western Union and relayed everything anyway. She packed me a bag: FIREMAN, LARGE. Thirty hours. Behave. She told me Julian isn’t coming, like I’d care, and I told her so.

choices.key: At the van Laney made sure you knew Julian isn’t coming. You asked her why you’d care.
response: At the open hatch, past the cooler, a pair of hands on a cargo strap stops pulling.
“Mm-hm,” Laney says. She looks across the roof of the van at Theo, who is coming back from the edge of the lot with the phone in his pocket, and Theo looks back at her.
The hands come off the strap. Kevin reaches up for the hatch, and it comes down on the loose tail of the strap, and he has to lift it and tuck the tail in and bring it down again.

choices.text: “Put it in the newsletter, Laney. I’m not a subscriber.”
choices.key: At the van Laney made sure you knew Julian isn’t coming. You told her to put it in the newsletter; you’re not a subscriber.
response: Laney doesn’t blink. “Noted, fireman.” She ticks something on her card that may or may not be on it.
At the hatch a pair of hands has stopped on a cargo strap. They hold, and then let go.
Kevin brings the hatch down. It shuts on the box from Oakland, riding on the cooler with its twine and its careful capitals.

choices.text: “I don’t care, Laney. Why would you think I would?”
choices.key: At the van Laney made sure you knew Julian isn’t coming. You told her you don’t care, and asked why she’d think you would.
response: At the open hatch the hands on the cargo strap stop.

Laney looks at him a second too long, as if she were checking a sum. “Just keeping the head count, fireman.” Her eyes go across the roof of the van to Theo. Theo, phone gone, has his hands in his blazer pockets and looks back.
Kevin brings the hatch down, and when it latches the back glass is facing all of them, the right way round: WHO DAT · 3 DAYS.

s07b.slug: THURSDAY · 9:10 PM · THE ANACAPA LOT, THE FAR END
body: Kevin’s last words over the hatch were *Five a.m.* and then, to Laney in particular, *Not Laney’s five.* At the other end of the lot now the Odyssey’s dome light goes off, and the van is a dark shape with a rosary in it.

Jack is down by the bike cage where the eucalyptus starts, the orange at his back and the dark going on down toward Del Playa in front of him. The tin is in the left pocket of the Carhartt. The Marlboros are in the right, and his right hand is in there with them, and has been since the hatch came down.

It went fine. A van packed, a seat assigned, a pie on a lap, and not a word to her or from her in an hour, in front of everybody. That’s how he wanted it, and how it went. He wants one anyway, the way he wants to sit down at the end of a Saturday close at the Anchor: in the legs first, then the hands, and last of all in anything that thinks. It’s twelve past nine on the RAZR. Nine-thirty is down the hill.

Down there Del Playa is getting its Thursday going, a bass line through somebody’s wall and a girl laughing on a balcony, and under it the surf at the bottom of the bluff. The wind comes up off the water through the cage with kelp in it.

choices.key: After the van, at the far end of the lot, you smoked one.
response: The lighter takes three tries in the wind off the water. He smokes half of it fast, standing at the cage, and puts it out on the post and drops it in the can. On the way down Del Playa toward the house he chews two pieces of the gum he pocketed out of FIREMAN, LARGE when he loaded it, which is the first thing in the bag he’s used, and behind him what’s left of the smoke goes back up the hill in the wind, the wrong way, toward the van.

He takes his hand out of the pocket without the pack in it. He starts down Del Playa toward the house with both fists shoved in the Carhartt, the left one around the tin and the right one around nothing, and walks, past the porch lights and the bikes chained to them, until the hands stop wanting anything.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven. Thursday night at the far end of the Anacapa lot, after the van: eleven.

response: He opens it under the last lamp. Eleven. He knows it’s eleven. He counts them anyway, with one finger, down the row, and the lid shuts on its little click, and the tin is back in the left pocket before he starts down Del Playa toward the house.
