s08.slug: THURSDAY · 9:35 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, SOL’S DARKROOM
s08.music: The Velvet Underground & Nico — “I’ll Be Your Mirror”
body: The porch light is off and the front door is on the latch; at Sol’s that means come in. Upstairs, Tomás’s door is shut. Somebody two streets over is having Thursday, and it comes through the walls of the house as bass and nothing else, a pulse in the plaster. The downstairs hall runs from the kitchen, where the light over the stove is on and the kettle sits in it, past the foot of the stairs, to the back of the house, where the door he has walked past all winter is shut on a red line of light along the floor.
He knocks.
“Wait —” Quick, through the wood, and a slosh, and a lid going down on a box. “Now. Fast.”
He gets in and gets the door shut behind him faster than he has ever shut a door in his life, and stands with his back against it.
Inside, there are two colors, and one of them is black.

The safelight hangs on its cord over the wet side and makes everything it touches red and gives everything it doesn’t to the dark. The room was a sleeping porch once; he can tell by the windows that aren’t there anymore, plywood where they used to be and blackout cloth stapled over the plywood, and the ceiling sloping down toward the yard. Along the right wall, a utility sink, and three trays in a row on a counter of bare plywood, and a sour bite of vinegar he knows from the peppers in Nonna’s cellar. Along the left, the dry side: old Formica, the enlarger standing on its column with its head bowed, a box of paper with its lid on, and a turntable with a record going around, a woman singing low and level over a guitar, no hurry in her anywhere. On a shelf above the trays a darkroom timer ticks off whatever she has set it for. Overhead, corner to corner, a clothesline, with prints hanging from it by wooden clothespins and dripping on the boards. Under the line, against the back wall where the porch railing must have been, at the end of the dry counter, an iron daybed with a moving blanket thrown over the mattress.

body.title: Taped inside the darkroom door, in marker
body.text: SKYE — DON’T TOUCH: The enlarger lens. The Nikon’s light meter (it lies. I know. Leave it). The box that says FIBER. My negatives. The fuse box (not yours either). CLOSE THE PAPER BEFORE THE DOOR. The daybed is not a shelf. — SOL

body: Skye is at the trays in a black rubber apron over a T-shirt, sleeves shoved past her elbows, her hair knotted on top of her head with a pencil through it and a pair of plastic tongs in one hand. She comes over and looks up at him under the light, and stops.
“Your eyes are black,” she says. “I’ve been in here since eight looking at you in black and white, and you walk in and it turns out you don’t have any blue in you either.”
“It’s the light.”
“That’s what everybody says about their eyes.” She goes up on her toes and kisses him, her fingers on his jaw smelling of vinegar, and drops back down. “Come look. You’re all over the place.”
He is. Down the line, pinned at the corners, it’s him.

The first one is him asleep. A mattress, a white wall, a man on his back with his face turned toward the lens and one hand tucked under his jaw, his mouth a little open, the St. Michael slid sideways into the hollow of his throat, the sheet down around his hips and his ribs long and pale and bare, with nothing drawn on them at all.
“Monday,” she says. “First light. That’s before the horse. That’s the canvas.”

He never heard the shutter. He looks at the man on the line, who is asleep the way kids sleep in the back seat coming home from a wake, gone, with every door unlocked, and who has no idea anybody is in the room.

The next are from the Point this afternoon, the roll’s last frames, still wet: the back of him walking down into the white water with Tomás’s nine feet of emergency under one arm and the wetsuit rolled to his waist, his shoulders gone white in the print where the sun was on them.
“Still a procession,” Skye says.

After those, the headland for Fenner: the rocks with the white water wrapped around their feet, the old light dark on top, the low wall along the cliff and the cross a small pale mark against it. “Fenner’s,” she says, and moves him on.

Apart from the rest, on a window screen laid across two sawhorses, the dry ones. On top is the swing. Tuesday, the porch, right after Danny’s call, shot through the screen door, so there is a faint grid of mesh over everything. Skye with her head back against the chain, laughing, one bare heel up off the boards. And Jack beside her, turned all the way to her, his mouth open in the middle of a word and the scar in his eyebrow hiked up, looking at her like she has just told him the end of a joke he has been waiting on since grade school.
There are pictures of him all down Ma’s upstairs hall on Glenwood: school pictures, First Communion, the Mooney jersey. None of them has that face in it.

“Tomás,” Skye says. “He was inside the screen door with his coffee. He never said a word. I didn’t know till the roll came up.” She is looking at the print, not at him. “That face. You don’t do it when anybody’s watching.”
“You took the first one while I was asleep.”
“I did.”
“That’s a little — ”

“That’s why it’s good.” She goes back to the trays and fishes the last of the Point out of the fixer and into the wash, the tongs clicking. “Every picture of me since I was a kid was posed and paid for. Chin down. Give me sad. They want you less tan. I’ve been shot by the best people in the business, and do you know what a camera tells the truth about? Light. Light, and what the client paid.” She pins the print up by one corner and it starts to drip. “These ones are true. Because you didn’t know. The only honest thing a camera ever did was catch somebody who wasn’t ready.”
“That’s backwards.”
“Of course it is. You’re here.”

He leans against the dry counter, minding the enlarger, minding Sol. “A true picture’s not one you take. Sixth Station. Every Friday in Lent at St. Brigid’s there’s a plaster woman on the wall with a towel held open in both hands and a face on it. Veronica. She wipes his face on the way up the hill and he leaves it on the cloth. For centuries that’s the picture of him people walked to Rome to see, and she didn’t take it. He gave it to her. They called it the *vera icon*. The true image.” He shrugs. “Her name probably came from the picture, not the other way around. But that’s the idea. True is given.”
“You had to say *probably*.”
“It’s in the contract. Philosophy major.”

She takes a sheet out of the box and puts the lid back on, and lays the sheet in the easel under the enlarger, and switches the lamp on for a count she keeps under her breath, and off. She slides the blank paper into the developer and rocks the tray with the tongs, slow, a little wave going end to end.
“Watch,” she says. “This is the part nobody takes.”
White paper under the liquid, nothing on it, and nothing, and then a gray where a jaw would be.
“There’s your jaw,” she says, rocking. “There’s the scar. There’s — ”

She stops. The paper goes on without her. His mouth comes up out of the white, closed eyes, the medal in his throat: it’s Monday again, closer, just the face, asleep in a tray of chemicals on Sol’s counter under a red bulb, and Skye stands over it with the tongs in her hand and doesn’t move it on to the next tray.
She lays the tongs across the end of the tray. “Everything true about anybody is stolen.”

body.text: “You stole me in a den in Montecito. I was reading for a part and you took the grandmother off me.”
body.else: “You stole me in a den in Montecito.”

choices.text: “A true picture’s one somebody gives you.”
response: “A true picture’s one somebody gives you,” he says, and stays on it.
She looks at him across the red. She reaches up and unpins the canvas from the line, him asleep, still dripping, and holds it out. “Then I’m giving you this one.”
“That one’s yours,” he says. “You were up first.”

She keeps it in her hand. She pins it back where it was. From the screen on the sawhorses she takes the swing, dry and curling at one corner, turns it face down on the Formica, and with a grease pencil out of the apron pocket she writes across the back in her capitals while he watches — NOT FOR POSTING — and hands it to him. He opens Hale’s *Moviegoer* to the middle and lays it in between two pages of Hale’s pencil and shuts the book on it.
“Professionally.” She takes a clothespin off the end of the line and clips it to his collar, a price tag.

She lifts the swing off the screen and hands it to him face down. It’s already written on, in grease pencil, in her capitals, a little smeared at the end where her wrist went through it: NOT FOR POSTING.
“I did that at eight,” she says. “Before you knocked. I’m a planner.”
He opens Hale’s *Moviegoer* to the middle and lays it in between two pages of Hale’s pencil and shuts the book on it. He leaves the clothespin on.
She looks at it on the screen, the mesh over the two of them and the chain and her heel in the air.
“Tomás has an eye,” she says. “Don’t tell him.”
She lifts it off the screen and puts it in his hands face down. “Read the back.”
He tips it to the safelight. Grease pencil, her capitals. “Not for posting.”
“Like you mean it.”
“Not for posting.”
“Good. That’s the caption.” He opens Hale’s *Moviegoer* to the middle and lays it in between two pages of Hale’s pencil and shuts the book on it.

s08a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:20 PM · THE DARKROOM — THE DOOR
body: The record is coming to the end of a side. The print of him asleep is still lying in the developer where she left it, gone darker than she would have let it if she were still printing. She isn’t. She’s been sitting on the edge of the wet counter with her heels against the cabinet, telling him what the skin person in Burbank charges by the hour. “Two hundred dollars to look at my elbows and tell me they’re still elbows. I want that job. I would be so good at that job.” He says the elbows look fine to him. “You’re not licensed,” she says, and hops down.

She puts the lid on the box of paper first. She pushes it to the back of the dry counter, behind the enlarger. She crosses the little room, picks up the gallon jug of fixer from under the sink by its handle, opens the door, and sets the jug against it.

The hall comes in. Not much of it: the dark, and the bass from two streets over louder by half, and at the far end the light over the stove, reaching down the floorboards toward them in a long pale strip. After an hour of red it might as well be noon. It crosses the floor and climbs the side of the wet counter, and in the developer tray the print of him asleep goes gray all at once, and grayer, his face sinking back into it, and then it is a black sheet in a tray with nothing in it.
The prints on the line are fixed. They hang there dripping in the light from the hall, him and him and the headland and him.
“That one was mine anyway,” Skye says.
She stays in the doorway, the stove light down one side of her and the red down the other.
“Why the door?” he says.
“So you know it’s there.”
She leans on the frame with her arms folded and the jug at her ankle, and the bass from two streets over comes down the hall behind her.
He looks at the doorway. It’s a door. It’s a dark hall with a kettle at the end of it.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye propped the door open on purpose, so you’d know it was there. You shut it.
response: He crosses to it and moves the jug with his foot, and the door swings to on its own weight and takes the hall with it, and the red has the room again.
“Then that’s you,” she says.
She comes back across the room to him. On the turntable the record has run off the end of the side into the groove, and in the shut room the hiss of it going around is suddenly very loud.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye propped the door open on purpose, so you’d know it was there. You left it open.
response: He leaves it.
“Then we leave it,” she says.
She comes back across the room to him with the stove light on one shoulder and the red on the other, and from then on the hall is a dark doorway behind her with a little of the kitchen in it.

body: The needle rides the run-out groove, a hiss and a small catch, a hiss and a small catch, around and around.

body.text: Behind her the doorway stands open on the dark hall, a little of the stove light lying in it.
body.else: Behind her the door is shut, and a thread of stove light shows along the bottom of it and nowhere else.

body: Skye picks the tongs up off the wet counter and points them at him and drops into a man he hasn’t met — hoarse, two packs a day, a man who has been standing in a field with a bullhorn since before dawn — “Last setup, people. We are losing the — ”
She puts the tongs down.
She takes the apron off over her head and hangs it on its nail, and comes to him.

It’s ten-thirty. The van is at five and her flight is at six-forty, and from the first minute she moves as if she has done that sum and isn’t going to do it again. She doesn’t hurry. She doesn’t stop, either. She takes Hale’s *Moviegoer* out of his back pocket, with the swing in it, and sets it on the dry counter by the enlarger. She pushes the Carhartt off his shoulders and lets it go, and it lands heavy on the side with the pockets. She gets his T-shirt up and over his head and leaves his arms caught in it while she kisses the middle of his chest beside the medal, and then frees them. She kneels on Sol’s rubber mat and unlaces his boots, both of them, to the last eyelet, and he stands on one foot and then the other like a kid being got ready for church. His belt. His jeans. The rest. He lets her run it.

She stands up in front of him and takes off her own: the T-shirt, the bra, the jeans, the rest, folding nothing, dropping each thing where she stands. The safelight finds her collarbones and the undersides of her breasts and the points of her hips and the long run of her stomach and gives the rest of her to the dark. He has seen all of her by a lamp and in the afternoon and under bathwater and with a parking lot coming through his window. He has never seen her in one color. His hands are shaking. The room is warm; Sol keeps a space heater under the sink for the chemistry.

She walks him backward until the edge of the dry counter is across the small of his back, cold Formica, the enlarger’s column against his wrist, and goes down on her knees on the mat, and takes him in her mouth. Her mouth is hot and the counter is cold and he is caught between the two, and her other hand comes up and spreads on his stomach and holds him back against the Formica, and he lets himself be held.

The red is on her shoulders and in her hair. The knot comes down and the pencil falls out of it and rolls away under the counter, and neither of them goes after it. His hands go into her hair, and then, because he needs somewhere to put them that isn’t her, back to the counter on either side of him, his fingers hooked over the edge. She isn’t slow tonight. She is quick and sure and she knows exactly where he is, every second, and she takes him there fast, his head back against the plywood, the bulb swimming above him, his breath going ragged and then going altogether —
— and she stops.

She takes her mouth away and sits back on her heels with her hand on him, still, and looks up at him in the red with her lips wet and her chin up, and keeps him where he is, right at the edge, with nothing moving. She watches what that does to him. She doesn’t look away from any of it.
He says her name. It arrives in pieces.
“I know,” she says.

She comes up the length of him and kisses him, and takes his hand and walks him backward across the room to the daybed and puts him down on Sol’s moving blanket. The iron rail is cold against his shoulders. The blanket smells like the back of a truck.

She turns around above him. She puts a knee on either side of his shoulders and settles her hips down to his mouth, and bends over him and takes him into her mouth again, and for the first time it isn’t anybody’s turn.

Every other night it has been one of them and then the other: somebody giving and somebody getting, somebody saying what they want and somebody doing it. Now it’s both at once, and there is no room in him to think about her and be thought about at the same time, so he stops trying to think. He has her thighs in his hands, the backs of them trembling under his palms. He has the taste of her, salt and sharp, and the heat of her against his face, and the sound she makes going straight down into him so that he feels it more than hears it, and his own going up into her, and her hair spilling over his hips, and her heels pressing into the blanket on either side of his head. It is too much to do both, and they do both.

When he gets close she is ahead of him. She lifts her mouth off him and holds still, her cheek on his hip, breathing hard against his skin, and when he groans her name at the ceiling she says into his hip, “We’ve got till five,” and waits until he has come back down; and starts again. The second time it happens he feels her smile against him. The third time he understands what she is doing. So when her thighs start to shake against his ears and her hips start chasing his mouth, he eases off, slows, holds her there, and her fist comes down on the blanket by his knee, and the sound she makes into him is half complaint and half yes. And he starts again. She showed him, and he learns, and after that it is the two of them holding each other right at the edge and not letting either one over, again and again, until he has lost count of whose edge it is.

Overhead, the prints have been dripping all along. One lets go a fat cold drop off its corner — the back of him, walking into the Pacific — and it lands between her shoulder blades. She jerks, and laughs. It bursts out of her, loud and sudden, with her mouth open, and she claps a hand over it out of habit, and then takes the hand away and looks at it. “Nobody through the wall,” she says. “I forgot.” And she laughs out loud into Sol’s darkroom. Another drop hits his shin, and that sets her off again.
“Your face is dripping on me,” she says, when she can.
“You hung it there.”
“I hung it there,” she agrees, and puts her mouth back on him, still laughing, so that he feels the laugh too.

When she has her breath she turns around and comes up the length of him, skin on skin from his knees to his mouth, and lies along him, and her hair comes down around both their faces. Her back is wet with print water under his hands and cold, and she is hot everywhere else. The St. Michael is caught under her, pressed into his breastbone by her weight.
“I know what I said about the morning,” she says. “I’m changing it. It’s mine.”

body.text: “Tuesday you told me to ask you. I wouldn’t take it like that. I’m asking now.”
“Tuesday you said you didn’t know if you’d say no. I didn’t want to find out on your floor.”
“Tuesday you held me and talked about the swing. I let you.”
“Tuesday you said no before I could choose.”

body: Her mouth is close enough that he feels the words land. “I want you inside me, Jack. Tonight. In here. Before anybody has to go anywhere.”

The needle goes around in its groove. Over her shoulder, on the line, he is asleep with his ribs bare, dripping. Somewhere in him the front half of a Hail Mary starts up by itself, as it does at red lights and in hospital hallways, and doesn’t get past *full of*. Every no he has ever said to her, he said to this face. He looks up at it in the red, close enough to feel her breathe.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye asked, in so many words. You said yes.
response: “Yes,” he says.
It sounds the same in red as it would in any light. Her breath goes out of her against his mouth, and her forehead comes down to his and stays.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye asked. You answered by taking off your St. Michael and laying it on the counter.
response: He gets a hand in under her and lifts his confirmation medal over his head. The chain catches on his ear, and he works it free, and reaches past her off the edge of the daybed as far as his arm goes, to the dry counter by the enlarger, and lays it there.
The small sound of it on the Formica. She turns her head and watches it go down.

choices.key: In the darkroom Skye asked. You answered with her real name: Mary Catherine.
response: “Mary Catherine,” he says.

response.text: In 412 he gave her what Nonna said about it, *a good name for a wife*. Her face in the red changes at the name, and he can’t tell which of the two she’s hearing, his or Nonna’s.
response.else: Her face, in the red, at her own name.

response: She hears what he means by it. Her forehead comes down to his and stays.

response: “Skye — wait — ”

He gets as far as her name and the front of the next word, and finds she has gone still above him, her hand already closed around the St. Michael on its chain. Whatever he was going to say, she was there before it.

body.text: She is already still above him. Her knees are on Sol’s moving blanket on either side of his hips and her fist is shut around the St. Michael where it lies on his chest, and his *wait* arrives late, under her, into a room where she has already stopped. She breathes hard through her nose, in and out, her hair hanging down around both their faces with the red coming through it in strands, and she doesn’t move, and the breath goes on shaking in and out of her as if she’d run here.

She comes up over him, a knee on each side of his hips on Sol’s moving blanket, and reaches down and takes him in her hand. She brings him to her and holds him there, at the very edge of her, and does not come down — the closest the two of them have ever been, nothing inside her, nothing keeping it there but her hand and whatever she does next. Her free palm is flat and low on his stomach, and she doesn’t look away from his face. Then she goes still. Her breath stops, and starts again, shorter. Her eyes are on his chest: on the bare place on his breastbone, pale in the red, where the medal has hung since his confirmation. She lets go of him. She climbs off the daybed and crosses the little room to the dry counter by the enlarger, naked in the safelight, and lifts the St. Michael off the Formica by its chain, and comes back and drops it over his head herself. It catches on his ear, as it did coming off. She frees it, and sets it back where it lives with one knuckle, and kneels over him with her hand on it.

She comes up over him, a knee on each side of his hips on Sol’s moving blanket, and reaches down and takes him in her hand. She brings him to her and holds him there, at the very edge of her, and does not come down — the closest the two of them have ever been, nothing inside her, nothing keeping it there but her hand and whatever she does next. Her free palm is flat and low on his stomach, and she doesn’t look away from his face. Then she goes still. Her breath stops, and starts again, shorter. Her eyes are on his chest, on the St. Michael on its chain on his breastbone, red in the safelight like everything else in here. She lets go of him. Her hand comes up and closes over the medal.
“Not him,” she says, her fist around the medal. “I was never going to take him off you.”
“Not him,” she says. “Don’t take him off for me.”
“Not him,” she says, with the medal in her fist. “I’m not taking him off you.”

body: “No,” she says, in her own voice.
She says it close, into his face, with her hair still hanging down around them both, and afterward her mouth stays a little open, as though the word were bigger going out than it looked.

She lifts away and lies down beside him on Sol’s daybed, on her back under the line, her shoulder against his, and she stays. Their clothes are in one heap on the floor of the dry side, red on red, where she dropped them.
Everything stops with it. Her hands, his, the clock that has been running in both of them since he knocked.

The sweat on his chest goes cold first. Then the backs of his legs, where the moving blanket is rough, and the place on his hip where her knee was. He can smell her on his hands and on his mouth, and the vinegar from the wet side under that, and the hot dust of the safelight. Above them the prints of him hang in a row on their clothespins, the back of him on the Point three times over, getting smaller, and him asleep.

body.text: His body hasn’t heard. He lies there with his heart going hard enough to shake the iron frame and his hands open on the blanket, and the first thing he knows clearly, before anything else can arrive, is that he would have. The second thing is his breath, coming back into him slower than his heart, from somewhere outside the room, like it’s being returned.

He lies there with his heart going hard enough to shake the iron frame and his hands open on the blanket, and the first thing he knows clearly, before anything else can arrive, is that she was there before his word was. The second thing is his breath, coming back into him slower than his heart, from somewhere outside the room, like it’s being returned.

body: When he can, he turns on his side toward her. She lets him get his arm under her neck. She reaches down for the free half of Sol’s moving blanket and hauls it up over the two of them to the chin, brisk as a nurse, and tucks it in along his back with the side of her hand, and then she lies still under it with her shoulder in his armpit and her eyes open.

On the wet side the timer goes off. It has ticked under everything since he came through the door, and now it rings — a flat tin ring that doesn’t let up — for some print she left in the fixer an hour ago and forgot. They let it ring. It rings until it runs down, and after it the room is quieter than it was before anything started.
Skye lies looking up at the pictures of him.
“Well,” she says. “That’s never happened to me.”

He turns his head on the blanket. Her profile in the red: the slope of her nose, her mouth still open from breathing, a strand of hair stuck to her temple with sweat, and her eyes wide open on the line.
“You okay?”
“Ask me why,” she says.

So he asks her why. She finds his hand on the blanket and brings it over and puts it on her stomach under her own, where he can feel her breathing go up and down, slower now, and slower, and she takes her time.

s09b.slug: FRIDAY · 12:20 AM · THE DARKROOM — MARY KATE
body: The red can’t change; it’s a bulb on a cord. Over the daybed the prints have slowed to a drop every few minutes, and Sol’s moving blanket is over both of them now, quilted, smelling of a storage unit and faintly of the vinegar from the wet side. Skye lies along him with her head on his shoulder and one foot hooked over his ankle, and she is watching the line.

body.text: Through the propped door the hall runs off dark toward the kitchen, where the stove light is still on over the burners: a little yellow at the far end of the house, the only thing in sight that isn’t red.
body.else: The door is shut where he shut it, the jug of fixer against the wall where his foot put it, and the seam around the door is as red as the rest of the room.

body: “That print in the fixer,” he says. “The one the timer was for.”
“Ruined. Probably. Sol would know.” She doesn’t sound sorry. “It was you again. I’ve got plenty of you.”

“You have somewhere to be in the morning,” she says. “So do I. I said nowhere to be.” Her finger is drawing on his chest under the blanket, slowly, something with corners. “I said it in your room and I meant it, and tonight I changed it because I wanted to. I don’t do that. I don’t say a thing and then not.”
The finger stops.

body.text: “And then you said yes.”
“And then you took him off.”
“You said wait,” she says. “I heard it. I’d already stopped. Remember that part.”

body: He waits for her. The safelight hums on its cord, the only sound in the room.

body.text: “I wanted the yes,” she says. “I didn’t know till I had it that it was the part I wanted.”
body.else: “I wanted the yes,” she says. “I could feel it coming up in you. Another minute and I’d have had it.”

body: “The yes,” he says.

body.text: “Since November. Since the window seat. I’ve been asking you for it in every room in Santa Barbara County.” Her finger starts again, the corners. “And you gave it to me on a daybed in a darkroom with your pictures dripping on us. And I had it. And it was —” The finger stops at the end of a corner. “I didn’t need anything after it. I didn’t know that about myself.”
body.else: “Since November. Since the window seat. I’ve been asking you for it in every room in Santa Barbara County.” Her finger starts again, the corners. “And tonight it was right there, on a daybed in a darkroom with your pictures dripping on us. And it was —” The finger stops at the end of a corner. “I didn’t need to hear it. I didn’t know that about myself.”

body: He turns it over and can’t find the bottom of it. She tips her head back to look up at the print of him asleep — him on her mattress at first light with his ribs bare, upside down from here — and tells it, “You’ve been watching this whole time. Creep.”

To the real one she says, “Look where we are.” Her hand comes out from under the blanket and takes in the room: the bulb, the black cloth tacked over the plywood, the trays, the line of him. “A room built so nobody can see anything in it. Lights off. I said I wanted to be the good thing with the lights off.” The hand goes back under. “I’d still be the thing you tell him about through a screen. And Sunday you’re going to want to go up, in some church in New Orleans I’ll never see. I want you to be able to.”
He starts to say she isn’t, and she puts her fingertips on his mouth.
“Don’t make it nice. You were going to make it nice.”
He was. He lies there with it shut.
“Why the morning?” he says, when she takes the fingers away. “You keep coming back to the morning.”
She doesn’t answer right away.

“He called me Mary Kate,” she says. “My father. Before the Olsens ruined it.” Her cheek moves on his chest; it might be a smile. “What I gave you at the taquería was the version I can do. The juicer, the jar with PAT on it, the hand up on the catwalk. It’s all true. I can tell it without my voice doing anything.” Her hand has gone still on his ribs. “This is the part I kept. When they shot on location they wanted him there at five, so he left in the dark. One morning he came in and kissed me in my bed and said go back to sleep, Mary Kate. So I went back to sleep. I was four.”

“He didn’t come back,” she says. “Debbie says I made up the kiss. I told you I don’t remember any of it, and I don’t: not the stages, not the car seat, not him up a ladder.” Her thumb moves on his ribs. “I remember that. He smelled like coffee and the cold. That and a hand on a catwalk is all I have of him, and the hand is the one I tell.”
“Did you wait up?”
“For a while.” She thinks about it. “Then I got a call time of my own.”
She lifts her head off his chest and looks at him, close, the red on half her face and the other half dark.
“Everybody I’ve ever loved had a call time.”
He gets his hand into her hair and holds the back of her head, the hair still stiff at the roots from the Point.
“You at five,” she says. “Me at six-forty.” And she puts her head back down where it was.

So he tells her about the turnout on Highway 1 in August, the first day: his father swinging the Silverado into the gravel without a signal, leaving the engine running and the door open and the dinger going, and walking to the guardrail in his union windbreaker with his hands in his pockets, and standing there looking at the Pacific for the first time in fifty-one years. He didn’t say anything. Not then, not in the truck after, not for five months. “Till this afternoon,” Jack says. “On the phone from the garage. It was big, he says. It’s allowed.” He hears his father in it and lets it stand. “Five months to get to big. That’s how you know with him. When he doesn’t say anything, that’s the most he’s got.”
Skye lies with her ear on his chest and listens to it come up through him.

“And I’ve never had nowhere to be in the morning either,” he says. “Not one I can remember. There’s a shift on Glenwood Avenue, or a Mass, or a bus. My dad’s alarm went off at a quarter to five for twenty-six years.” He hears himself and keeps going. “In June it stopped. He still gets up at a quarter to five. He sits in the garage with the radio.”
“So nobody has to watch him not leave,” she says. And then: “Does he know? That you love him?”
“We don’t say it.” He looks up at the line. “He drove me across the country instead. Two plane tickets cost more than the truck’s worth. Then he drove it home alone.”
“That’s saying it,” Skye says. “That’s saying it with a truck.”
He has one more, and it’s the one he has been holding since the timer rang.

body.text: “What would you have done,” he says, “if I’d said no?”
body.else: “What would you have done,” he says, “if I’d got the rest of it out?”

body: “Asked again.” No hesitation in it at all. “Next week. On the phone from Burnaby, from a trailer. The night you got back. I’d always ask again, Jack. That’s the problem.” Her hand closes in the hair on his chest. “I’d never have stopped. So I did.”
He lies there with that, and gives her the only thing he has that’s as true as it.

body.text: “I’d have let you,” he says. “Tonight. I want you to know it was you. It wasn’t me holding anything.”
body.else: “I was going to stop it,” he says. “I want you to know that. I’d got as far as the word.”

body.text: “I know.” She doesn’t lift her head. “I was there, Jack. I was the one holding it.”
body.else: “I know.” She doesn’t lift her head. “I got there first, Jack. I was the one holding it.”

body: She lays her cheek on him again, under the line of prints, and talks to his chest.

“When you come back,” she says. “Whatever you’ve got. Whatever happens down there — the Saints, Mardi Gras, a float falls on you. You tell me. To my face.” Her fingers move on his chest. “Not in a text from Texas. You don’t lie. It’s why I can do any of this.”

response: “I promise,” he says.
Her arm comes across him under Sol’s blanket and settles there. “Okay,” she says into his chest.

She comes up on an elbow and looks at him in the red, and touches the scar through his eyebrow with one fingertip, and goes no further into it than that. Past her shoulder the line runs from the enlarger to the door, and halfway along it, where the swing hung, there’s a clothespin holding nothing.

choices.key: Skye asked for the truth, to her face, when you come back. You took her face in your hands and said yes.

She holds still for it with her eyes open. When he lets go she puts her head back down on his chest.

choices.key: Skye asked for the truth, to her face, when you come back. You told her you’ll be terrible at Mardi Gras — then, when she waited, you promised.

She lifts her head and looks at him until he says the rest. “I promise.”
“You’re going to be magnificent at Mardi Gras,” Skye says. “They’re going to give you a float. Call me from the float.”

s09c.slug: FRIDAY · 2:25 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — CALL TIMES
body: After the red, her overhead light is an assault: the white ceiling, the blue duvet, his own hands gone pink again. The three suitcases stand zipped by the door, biggest to smallest, a family waiting on a cab. The Saab’s keys sit on top of the jar of beach glass, and her white phone on the dresser says 2:25.

Skye is on the end of the bed in a gray hoodie and bare legs, pulling on socks and reading it off to him like a call sheet. “Santa Barbara at six-forty. San Francisco. Vancouver by lunch. A man at the bottom of the escalator holding a sign with somebody else’s name on it.”
“Passport,” she says, and slaps the front pocket of the hoodie, and it’s there. She’s done that twice since they came up the stairs.

Over her head on the shelf the O’Connor is back in its place, the spine broken white, the one with CON crossed out inside it. The room has been stripped down to what stays: the jar, the books, the bare end of the clothes rack, the window over the bed showing nothing but the room back.

Jack is on the floor with his back against the dresser, lacing his boots. Hale’s *Moviegoer* is in his back pocket with the print inside it. He told her in the hall where he’s going: Osei says whenever you knock; he was a doctor; he’s used to being woken.
“Tell him I said hi,” she says. “Your priest.” She hears it before he’s finished the first boot. “Don’t tell him I said hi. It’ll look like lobbying.”
“He’d take it as lobbying.”
“He’d bless it. He blesses everything. He blessed my candle and I didn’t even ask.” She gets the second sock on and sits with both hands around her ankle, watching him double-knot.
“You’re going to go tell him anyway.”

body.text: “I said yes.”
“I took him off.”
“I got close enough.”
“So the yes counts,” she says. “I read that one. The heart one.”
body.else: “So close counts,” she says. “I read that one. The heart one.”

body.text: “The yes is most of it.”
body.else: “Close is most of it.”

body: She thinks about that with her chin on her knee. Down the hall Tomás’s door is shut, and two streets over the party has finally given up.
“Then what did I stop, for you?”
He finishes the knot before he answers. “Thirty hours,” he says. “In a van, with that in it.”
She nods, slowly.
“Okay.”
She stands, crosses the room in her socks, and takes the keys off the jar. The glass in it shifts and settles. She holds the keys in her fist with the fob hanging out, and looks at him on her floor.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised.

choices.text: *Let her drive you up the hill.*

s09h.slug: FRIDAY · 2:45 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE LOT UNDER THE BELL TOWER
body: She has driven up Ocean Road with the top up and both hands on the wheel and no radio, past the Grove and the dark faculty houses and the turn for the harbor, and said nothing on the way but “Seat belt,” at the bottom of the hill, like his mother.

The lot under the bell tower holds Osei’s small car by the hall door and, now, the Saab, nosed in beside it with the engine running for the heat. Three suitcases ride in the back seat, belted in. She belted them. The big one has its handle up against the roof.
Behind the blue glass of the church a light is on low, over toward the side aisle: small, yellow, steady. Everything else in the building is dark except the red point by the tabernacle.
Skye has her wrists crossed on top of the wheel and her chin on her wrists, and she looks at the light with him. The heater blows on their shins.

A little over three hours ago, in a red room, he gave her his answer. Now he is about to walk across a parking lot and tell it to a priest, and she drove him to the door. He looks at her hands on the wheel, the rings, the knuckles, and can’t think of a thing to say about that which wouldn’t be a joke.
“I’ll be here,” she says. “I’m good at waiting in cars. It’s most of my job.” She tips her head at the back seat without lifting it off her wrists. “And I brought company.”
“You could sleep.”
“I could. I won’t.” She turns her face on her wrists to look at him. “Go on. He’s up. Look at him, up.”
He leans across the gearshift to kiss her, and she stops him with one hand on his chest, on the St. Michael through his shirt, not pushing, just there.
“Kiss me coming out.”
He looks at her for that, and she looks back, in the green of the dash lights, with her hand where it is, until he nods. She takes the hand back and folds it on the wheel with the other one.

He gets out. The door shuts on the heater, and the cold coming down off the hill gets into his collar on the first step, and across the lot the light behind the blue glass is still on, waiting for whoever knocks.

s09w.slug: FRIDAY · 2:40 AM · OCEAN ROAD, ON FOOT
body: At the front door she stands on the sill in her socks with the hall light behind her, the porch dark and Sol’s swing hanging still at the end of it. She has his collar in one fist.
“I’ll see you at five,” she says. “I’ll be the one with three suitcases.”
She kisses him there, quick, up on her toes on the sill, and lets go of the collar with a little shove that starts him down the steps.

Del Playa this late is wrecked and quiet: red cups in the ice plant, a couch on a garage roof with a sleeping bag on it, somebody’s bike lying in the street with its front wheel still turning in the wind off the water. Under the bluff the surf breaks and drags its stones back. He goes up through Las Olas past the jasmine on the chain-link, and then the houses stop and the Grove starts, and the eucalyptus is giving its smell up into the cold — menthol, and the other thing, and the rain they haven’t had.

Ocean Road has no shoulder worth the name. He walks the white line. Hale’s *Moviegoer* rides in his back pocket with the print inside it, and every step he can feel the corner of it through the book and the denim, a stiff little edge against his hip.

body.text: He said yes. He doesn’t try to make it smaller on the way up. In twenty minutes he’ll have to say it to a man behind a screen, and there’s no better word for what he said than the one he used, so he carries that one up the hill.

He didn’t say anything. He took his medal off and put it on a counter, and that was an answer, and in twenty minutes he’ll have to put it into words for a man behind a screen. He tries a few on the way up. None of them is smaller than the thing.

He got as far as *wait*, and she was already there. He doesn’t let that make the rest of it smaller on the way up. In twenty minutes he’ll have to say all of it to a man behind a screen, the room and the blanket and how close, and he carries it up the hill in the words he’ll use.

body: He says the St. Michael prayer under the eucalyptus like a bouncer going down a list — *be our defense against the wickedness and snares* — and gets all the way to *the ruin of souls* without losing it.

One car comes up behind him: a pizza Civic with its sign still lit on the roof at this hour, the driver hunched over the wheel like he’s reading it. Its lights throw Jack’s shadow a hundred feet up the road ahead of him and then take it back, and its taillights go around the curve and leave him the dark.

The road climbs. At the top of the hill St. Brendan’s is a black shape against a sky only a little less black, the bell tower going up out of it, and before he has reached the courtyard gate he can see it: one light on behind the blue glass, low, over toward the side aisle, small and yellow, the only lit window on the hill.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 3:05 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S — BEHIND THE SCREEN

body.text: He comes up the steps from the lot with the Saab idling behind him under the bell tower, its parking lights on and its heater going for the girl inside it, three suitcases in the back. The hall door is on the latch.
body.else: He comes in off Ocean Road on foot with the cold on the shoulders of the Carhartt and the eucalyptus still on his hands from the fence at the top of the hill, where he stopped to get his breath. The hall door is on the latch.

body: Inside, the church is blue and black. The streetlight on Ocean Road comes through the west glass in long pale bars across the pews, and up front, past all of it, the lamp by the tabernacle is burning, red and small as the end of a cigarette. It is First Friday. Somewhere in the dark there is a heart on a holy card in a pew rack, on fire and wrapped in thorns. At the back by the doors the little light over the confessional door is on, and the card under it has grown a line.

body.title: The card on the confessional door
body.text:
KNOCK (GENTLY)
(AND PROMPTLY)
(ALL NIGHT TONIGHT — TRAVELERS)

body: The third line is in Osei’s hand, the capitals leaning uphill.

He is halfway down the side aisle when the door opens and Kevin steps into the light in his quarter-zip, his mother’s car key on its ring around one finger. He wets his hand in the font and crosses himself and sees Jack, and stops.
“He’s got a thermos,” Kevin says, at church volume.
“Good.”
“Couldn’t sleep.”
“Same.”
Kevin opens his mouth, and whatever is in it he trades for something smaller. “Four-forty-five. He’s blessing the car.”
The key goes around his finger once more and into his fist. He goes out by the hall door, and his sneakers go down the steps fast, and the lot has him.

Jack knocks gently. On the far side a chair takes a man’s weight and a cap comes off something with a squeak, and he goes in and kneels on the worn place in the dark, his forearm on the ledge, the Prodigal Son on the back of the door behind him with his face buried in his father’s coat. Hale’s *Moviegoer* is in his back pocket with the two of them in it, and kneeling bends it to the shape of him. Through the linen comes the smell of coffee, black and burnt, night-shift coffee.

body.text: His fingers smell of her stop bath. He puts a hand up to his collar and finds the clothespin still on it, and takes it off, and holds it.
body.else: His fingers still smell of her stop bath. He can’t get it off them; he has stopped trying.

body: “You’re up, Father.”
“My body still believes it is a resident,” Osei says. “It is the only part of me that does.”
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been a day and a half since my last confession.”
The cap goes back on the thermos. “Thirty-one hours. I have had patients come back sooner, but they were bleeding.”

He gives it in the short words, with the honest verbs. Where he was, and who with, and what they did there, both of them, all of it. A room built for the dark, and she wasn’t supposed to be in it either. None of it takes long and none of it is small, and on the other side of the linen the chair doesn’t move once.

body.text: Then the worst, last, because that is how he was taught, and flat. “She asked me. In so many words.” He makes himself finish it. “I started to say wait. She’d already stopped.”

Then the worst, last, because that is how he was taught, and flat. “She asked me. In so many words. I didn’t say anything. I took my medal off and put it on the counter. That was my answer.” And the end of it, the part he walked up here carrying. “She’s the one who stopped.”
Then the worst, last, because that is how he was taught, and flat. “She asked me. In so many words. I said yes.” And the end of it, the part he walked up here carrying. “She’s the one who stopped.”
“And Michael,” Osei says. “Where did you leave him?”
“On the counter. She put him back on me.”
The chair is quiet. “Then she knows something about you,” Osei says, “that you have mislaid.”

body: “She stopped,” Osei says back to him, evenly, and then says nothing else, and makes him kneel in it.

Under the floor the furnace comes on with a thump and a long breath up through the grate by the kneeler, warm on his ankles. He kneels there with *she stopped* in the little room and nothing to put next to it.

body.text: “On Wednesday you told me you were closer than you had ever been to not wanting to,” Osei says. “Now you know exactly how close.”
“On Wednesday you told me you would try,” Osei says. “I believed you. I still do; that is not the question.”
“On Wednesday you promised me this week,” Osei says. “It is still this week.”

body: “She said Sunday,” Jack says. “She wants me to be able to go up. She’s been reading about it.”
“Yes. Twice in a week someone who never made you a promise has kept yours for you.”
“I know.”

body.text: “Do you? You have made her the keeper of your vow, Jack. She never took one. In January I told you that if you make her the answer you will make her the occasion. This is the same mistake with a kinder face.” The beads move in the dark. “You love her. I do not doubt it; I have heard you say so, out loud, in this box. Then do not hand her the hardest part of you and drive to Louisiana.”
body.else: “Do you? You have made her the keeper of your vow, Jack. She never took one.” The beads move in the dark. “You love her. I do not doubt it; I have heard you say so, out loud, in this box. Then do not hand her the hardest part of you and drive to Louisiana.”

body: “It’s the best thing anybody’s ever done for me, Father.”
“I believe you. It is why I am awake.” The chair creaks. “A man cannot live on someone else’s no. It is not his to eat.”
Jack looks at the linen.

“Yesterday’s Gospel,” Osei says. “He sent them out two by two and told them to take nothing for the journey. Not bread, not a bag, not a second tunic. I would add: not a door you mean to come back through.”
Osei unscrews the thermos and pours, and drinks. “Kevin telephoned me yesterday to ask me to bless his mother’s car. He asked me also to pray for its atmosphere.”

Behind Jack the Prodigal Son goes on hiding his face in his father’s coat. Osei does not wait to see if anything comes back. The furnace shuts off. In the quiet Jack can hear the man on the other side of the linen breathing, slow, a man who has sat up with a great many people at this hour and has not yet been the first to leave.
“Are you sorry, Jack? Or are you sorry it stopped?”

body.text: He knows what he is supposed to say. He can feel the shape of it in his mouth, worn smooth from Glenwood Avenue and St. Brigid’s and every Saturday since. And under it, the red, and her weight, and her forehead on his, and the word he said in that room, which some part of him has not stopped saying yet. He kneels between the two with her stop bath on his hands.

He knows what he is supposed to say. He can feel the shape of it in his mouth, worn smooth from Glenwood Avenue and St. Brigid’s and every Saturday since. And under it, the red, and her weight, and the small sound of the medal going down on the Formica, which some part of him is still setting down. He kneels between the two with her stop bath on his hands.

He knows what he is supposed to say. He can feel the shape of it in his mouth, worn smooth from Glenwood Avenue and St. Brigid’s and every Saturday since. And under it, the red, and her weight, and the yes that was coming up in him behind the *wait*, which some part of him has not stopped meaning. He kneels between the two with her stop bath on his hands.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. I told him I called a friend a liar at a table, and went for the places that hurt. Two sins, he said, and I confessed the one I’m sure of. He said he’d be less sure, if he were me. I told him I’d spoken for him on Monday. He let most of it stand: what’s good between us is good, and the near occasion was the room and the hour and the door. He said I took his daylight at noon with the door shut. Neither one cancels the other. And if I make her the answer, I’ll make her the occasion. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight. The Fourth Sunday: a prophet’s never welcome in his own country. Skye watched me go up. At the door he said “Skye,” and she said “Father,” and he looked at me about as long as a handshake. He didn’t say anything. Candlemas: Simeon held the child and let himself be let go. At the door he said, “I saw your concert.” Wednesday at eight I told him all of it, and the song. Ghana has seen it. s10a.slug: FRIDAY · 3:40 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE FRONT STEPS
body: The courtyard is black, and the olive trees are a blacker shape in it, and the cold comes up out of the top step through the seat of his jeans. Down the hill the Anacapa lot is a puddle of orange, and in the middle of it, small from here, the shape of Kevin’s mother’s van, loaded and waiting. Behind him the little light over the confessional door is still burning for whoever comes next.

body.text: He says Mark 6 on the step anyway, as much as St. Brigid’s left in him: two by two, and a walking stick, and no bread and no bag for the road. It’s nobody’s penance. He says it to the end of what he has.
body.else: He starts the penance on the step, aloud, to the dark courtyard, as much of it as Osei gave him: two by two, and a walking stick, and no bread and no bag for the road. A house, and stay in it. The rest is in a book he doesn’t have on him.

body.text: The Saab is where he left it under the bell tower, the engine running, the parking lights making two orange smudges on the stucco. Skye is asleep against her own window with her coat pulled up to her chin and her cheek on the glass, and her breath has made a small gray country on it. He gets in. The heat is thick and smells like the vents and like her. She wakes when the door shuts, without opening her eyes, and tips her face up off the glass, and he kisses her. “There,” she says. Then she sits up and drives him down Ocean Road and into the Anacapa lot, past the dark van, to the far end by the eucalyptus, and parks, and leaves the heater on. She tips her head back against the window and shuts her eyes again.
“Did he take it?”
It’s the only thing she asks.
“No,” Jack says. “He blessed me.”

She opens her eyes. She looks at him across the gearshift, in the orange coming through the windshield. She asks nothing else. She reaches over and puts her hand on the back of his neck, warm from the coat, and leaves it there.
Her hand goes heavy. She sleeps against the window till a quarter to five, and he doesn’t.
“Yeah.”
She nods with her eyes shut. Her hand comes off her lap and finds his on the gearshift by feel, and covers it, and stays.

She sleeps against the window till a quarter to five, and he doesn’t. The *Moviegoer* is on his knee, shut, still curved from the kneeler. The clock on the dash says 3:52, and then it says other things.

Delgado is dark except the lobby. In 412 Theo is a long shape under the duvet with his back to the room. Jack doesn’t undress. He lies down on top of his made bed in the Carhartt and his boots with Hale’s book on his chest, the swing inside it, NOT FOR POSTING face down against his breastbone through two hundred pages, and looks at the ceiling until Theo’s alarm, and doesn’t sleep.
At 4:20 Theo’s alarm goes off and plays its little tune twice through.
“I’m up,” Theo says, from the dark.

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 4:45 AM · THE ANACAPA LOT — THE BLESSING OF TRAVELERS
body: The lamps over the Anacapa lot have burned all night and look it: a tired orange on the asphalt and the bike cage, on the eucalyptus at the far end, on the dew gone gray across every windshield in the rows. It is cold enough to see. Kevin’s mother’s van sits loaded where they left it, hatch down, and the back glass faces the lot the right way round: WHO DAT · 3 DAYS, in white, a day out of date since midnight. Jack hasn’t slept, and his eyes know it.

body.text: Skye wakes up against her window as if somebody had called her name from the next room, sits up, and puts the Saab in gear. She drives the length of the lot with the headlights on, slowly, past the van and the people standing at it, and swings around at the lot’s mouth so the nose points out at Ocean Road, and stops. They get out together, one on each side, and the two doors shut at the same time, two flat sounds. At the van Laney’s head comes around for it, and Theo’s, and Kevin’s. Behind them, through the back windows, three suitcases ride with the belts across them.

Jack is at the hatch in last night’s clothes, his hands in the Carhartt, when the Saab comes in off the road with the top up and the headlights on and noses into the space beside the van. Three suitcases ride in the back seat with the belts across them. Skye gets out in a long black coat with her hair knotted up off her neck and a paper cup in each hand from the 7-Eleven on the loop, comes straight to him, puts one in his hand, and keeps the other.

body: She looks the scene over — the van, the orange, the little clouds of breath going up from everybody, the hour on all of them. “Look at this,” she says. “Everybody’s here before call.” She shakes her head at them. “I’d hire every one of you.”

Kevin has the key on one finger and his quarter-zip zipped to the chin. Theo is sitting on the back bumper in a camel coat with his eyes open on nothing, turning his phone over and over in his hand. Laney is in her Pi Lam sweatshirt with the sleeves pulled down over her hands and sunglasses pushed up on her head at a quarter to five in the morning. Margot is already in her seat, middle left, with the door slid open and her Docs on the running board and Gloria’s box across her knees, both hands on the lid. Past the roof of the van, on the far side, Lena stands by the door to the way-back with her arms folded in a gray hooded sweatshirt. That much comes in at the edge of his eye. He doesn’t look again, and it isn’t hard.
Kevin goes down the van with the key, pointing it at each of them in turn, his lips moving, and lands on Skye. “Seven,” he says. Then: “Six. Sorry — six. There are seven seats. It gets in your head.”
“Keep one warm,” Skye says.
On the far side of the van Lena speaks, to Kevin. “Kevin. Does he have his license.”
Kevin doesn’t turn around. “Jack. License.”
Jack takes out his wallet and holds it up open over the roof of the van, at the lamps, and puts it back.
“He has his license,” Kevin says.

Father Osei’s small car comes down off Ocean Road with one headlight brighter than the other and parks across two spaces. He gets out in a black anorak and rubber boots to the shin, an aspergillum in one hand and a squeeze bottle of water in the other, and crosses the lot at the pace of the limp, as though five in the morning were a perfectly ordinary hour to be out in a parking lot with equipment.
Kevin puts a hand on the roof of his mother’s van. “Still pretty blessed, Father.”
“It went to Big Sur and came back,” Osei says, unscrewing the head of the aspergillum to fill it from the bottle. “That is all I promise.”
Over the van his eyes find the Saab, the three suitcases belted into it, and then Skye.
“You are traveling too, Skye?”
“Vancouver. Six-forty.”
“Then stand with them.”
She looks at the six of them, and back at him. “What’s my blocking?”
“Stand,” Osei says. “Standing is very ancient.”
“I can do ancient,” Skye says.

So they stand, a ragged circle at the front of the van in the light of the parking lamps Kevin has switched on for it. Theo comes off the bumper. Margot brings the pie. Skye takes the place Osei points her to, between Jack and Theo, and bows her head, and closes her eyes. Jack, beside her, sees it close: her lashes down in the orange, the knot of her hair, her breath going out of her slow and white. Across the hood Lena makes the sign of the cross. Jack makes his.
While Osei talks, Jack puts in one of his own, underneath, short: the six-forty out of Goleta, all the way up, and down again in two weeks.

“In the book of Tobit,” Osei says, “a young man is sent on a long road, and an angel walks with him there and back, and does not tell him who he is until they are home. May that one go with you.” The aspergillum rests against his boot. “Lord, go before them on the road. Stay with them in the house where they stop. And bring them home to us, all of them — at sixty-five.”
“Amen,” says the circle. Theo’s comes a half second late, and very sincere.

body.text: The water next. Osei goes around with it, a flick of the wrist at a time: the hood, the windshield, the hatch with its white letters, the far side of the van, and then the people, one by one along the circle, Kevin and Margot and the pie and Laney and Theo, and Jack, the same water out of the same bottle as everybody’s. Some of it goes in at his collar and runs down his back, cold.

“Does it work on Saabs?” she asks.

Osei looks across at the Saab and its three suitcases belted in, and goes over to it in his boots, and gives the hood two flicks of the wrist and the windshield one. “It is Swedish,” he says, coming back. “It may need more.”
“It’s GM,” Jack says.
“Don’t,” Skye says, still smiling at her car.
She goes down the line.
At the windshield she stops and leans toward the glass, and reads the card taped to the dash beside the chart. “Sixty-five,” she tells Kevin.
“Not sixty-six,” Kevin says, as if it were in the Creed.
“Ted.”
“Callender.”

Theo hugs her longer than a hug usually runs, his chin on her shoulder, and says something into her hair that only she gets. Over her shoulder his face is turned toward the van with its eyes open, and Jack, looking straight at it, can’t read it. Theo lets go of her and is Theo again. “Break a leg. Figuratively. I’ve read the cast insurance.”
“Send me the pilot,” Margot says, over the pie. “I want to see what they do to you.”
“I’ll send you the cut with the notes on it,” Skye says. “You’ll agree with all of them.”
Laney watches her come with the sleeves pulled down over her hands.
“Nice glasses,” Skye says.
Laney brings the sunglasses down off her head onto her nose, in the dark, and looks at her through them. “Knock ’em dead up there.”
Skye goes around the hood to the far side. Jack doesn’t follow her past the headlight; he hears it.
“Have a good trip, Lena. Win your game.”
“Safe flight.”
The sliding door rolls shut on the far side. Through the van’s glass, in the way-back, a gray hood goes up.

Skye comes back around the hood with her hands in her coat pockets, taking her time, the last name on her list. She stops in front of him and looks up at him with the orange on one side of her face. He has been up since yesterday morning, and he is sure of exactly one thing in this lot, and it is standing in front of him with holy water in its hair.
“Read me the margins,” she says. “In that book of yours. Whoever wrote all over it. On the phone, from Texas — not the book, I can buy the book. Them.”
“They’re Hale’s.”
“Then definitely them.”
“Some of them are rude.”
“Those first.”
“Two weeks,” she says. “Then I come back. That’s how this one goes.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. We went south.
